#1757. The Rock of London: Looking back at John Terry’s Chelsea FC career

Home » Home 2 » The Rock of London: Looking back at John Terry’s Chelsea FC career

At the start of this season, John Terry leaving Chelsea was the last thing on anyone’s mind. All was rosy at Stamford Bridge, the home of the newly crowed English champions. In over 21 years at the club, there was no indication that Terry would not retire a Chelsea man.

The Blues’ skipper’s announcement in January 2016, then, came as a shock to the Chelsea faithful, bringing notice to the seemingly premature — even if inevitable — fall of the curtain on a legendary career.

After making his debut in the League Cup against Aston Villa late in 1998, John Terry made sporadic appearances under Gianluca Vialli, before joining Nottingham Forest on a short loan spell. He broke into the first team in 2000-01, when manager Claudio Ranieri handed him 22 Premier League appearances during a season that the 20-year-old would finish as the club’s Player of the Year.

It would be the first of several achievements to come.

Terry’s importance to the team grew as Ranieri relied on his partnership with then-captain Marcel Desailly to mastermind Chelsea’s progression from a fashionable mid-table club to a Champions League team that meant business. They received a major shot in the arm when Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich bought the club in 2003. It was also a significant year in Terry’s international career as he made his England debut against Serbia and Montenegro in June.

The season that followed saw Chelsea finish above perennial winners Manchester United for the first time in Premier League history, and defeat Premiership invincibles Arsenal en route to the club’s first Champions League semifinal. Terry ended the season making a first of four appearances in the PFA Team of the Year, and went to Portugal for the European Championships having displaced Sol Campbell as England’s first choice centre-back.

In the summer of 2004, Chelsea brought in Jose Mourinho, who was fresh from winning a treble with the unfancied FC Porto and raring to take on bigger challenges. The 23-year-old Terry was named captain as Chelsea embarked on the most successful period in the club’s history. In the three seasons that followed, Chelsea won 2 league cups, 2 Premier League titles and the FA Cup — success built on a core of John Terry, Frank Lampard, Petr Cech and Didier Drogba, Chelsea’s ‘old guard’.

This was also a period when Terry picked up several individual accolades. He was named PFA Player of the Year in 2005, the first defender to win the award since Paul McGrath in 1993. He would make a first of five consecutive appearances in the FIFPro World XI in 2005, as well as a first of four appearances in the UEFA Team of the Year.

He was also voted Chelsea’s Player of the Year for the second time in his career in 2006. Steve McClaren, hired as England manager after an underwhelming 2006 World Cup, named the Chelsea skipper as England captain.

Terry was now, beyond argument, one of football’s best.

However, more testing times were to come.

September 2007 saw the departure of Mourinho after a falling out with the club board. The season itself promised much but left a Chelsea squad dejected on three occasions as they saw the League Cup, the Premier League and the Champions League trophies go elsewhere.

For the European Cup in particular, Terry was left with no one but himself to blame as he slipped for the crucial penalty, a moment he has said will haunt him forever. Chelsea and Terry experienced further European heartbreak the following season as Tom Henning Ovrebo had a refereeing performance to forget at Stamford Bridge, handing Barcelona a berth in the final and eventually the trophy.

In early 2010, when he was revealed as the English footballer who had an affair with Vanessa Perroncel, Wayne Bridge’s ex-girlfriend — a horrendous personal error that cost him his status as England captain — it made him the perennial recipient of passionate booing across English grounds. After the revelation, Chelsea travelled to Burnley. Amidst a frosty reception, he scored a late winner to put Carlo Ancelotti’s side back on track in the title race, one they would go on to win in some style. All of this typified John Terry — imperfect, but unshakeable.

Terry had built an unflappable reputation as a top class defender, leader and hard man. He said about himself, “I still say if the ball is there to be won I will go for it, whether with my head or whatever, and if it means us scoring or stopping a goal, I won’t think twice.”

The period that followed, however, was not good for Chelsea or their captain. The team finished the 2010-11 season trophyless, and Carlo Ancelotti paid for it with his job. This was the first of two times in Terry’s career where he and his club would have an extremely underwhelming season following a dominant one, and it also marked the first attempt to phase him out of the first team.

New manager Andre Villas-Boas attempted to introduce a high defensive line that left Terry exposed on a number of occasions, and saw the young Portuguese manager fall back on quicker defenders to implement his system. He was also determined to make lesser use of Frank Lampard and displace Didier Drogba with Fernando Torres. These were unpopular moves that led to poor results and eventually his sacking. Terry was not helped by another personal abberation, mouthing racial profanity at Anton Ferdinand of QPR, an act that saw him land a lengthy ban and damage his position in the England squad almost beyond repair.

Interim manager Roberto Di Matteo reinstated the old guard, and was rewarded with the ultimate prize — the first Champions League in Chelsea’s history.

Terry retired from international football following EURO 2012, leaving him to focus on his club career. However, further rotation was to follow during the reign of Rafael Benitez, who played Terry only in games of lesser importance. This was something he could do with relative impunity owing to the fact that his stock could not have fallen any further among Chelsea fans.

The writing was seemingly on the wall, however. Unsavoury incidents were fresher in the memory than individual accolades, the skipper was out of favour for two seasons running, and was well over 30 years of age. Was John Terry done?

Mourinho did not share the views of Benitez and Villas-Boas. Where they saw a slowing, easily-exposed has-been, he saw an experienced warrior with an excellent reading of the game who could form a title-winning partnership with the quicker Gary Cahill.

Terry grabbed the opportunity he was handed with gusto, performing with excellence in Mourinho’s lower defensive block. The English pair formed the core of a defence that would go on to win the club’s fourth Premier League title in 2015, leading the table from the opening day to the end. It was a landmark achievement for Terry in particular as he played every minute of a league campaign for the first time in his career, aged 34.

Once again they tried to put him down. Once again he fed off it and rose tall.

Chelsea did not start the defence of their title well at all, gathering just 4 points from the first 4 matches. Mourinho, who asked Terry to take the club on his shoulders in 2004 and stood by him for two seasons in his second stint, hauled off his skipper at half-time at the Etihad in the second game of the season, and began to rotate him out of the team, giving an increasing number of starts to the young Kurt Zouma.

The season did not take much of a turn for the better even under interim manager Guus Hiddink, particularly in a defensive sense as the Blues continued to let in goals during a meek climb to the top half of the table, with or without Terry in the side.

A sending off at the Stadium of Light following an injury layoff is not the kind of ending that the fans desired for their beloved captain, who has emerged from the dugout 703 times in Chelsea colours and has been the face of the club through the most successful period in their history.

Offered a new deal by the club last week, the skipper responded, “The contract extension the club has offered me is a different role and I hope everyone will understand I want to take the time to consider it carefully before making a decision.” While fans will hope — for reasons emotional as well as those to do with football — that Terry stays on, the chances look slim.

Should the captain leave the ship, the Blues supporters’ emotions are best summed up by a certain banner that embellishes the Shed End: Captain, Leader, Legend.

#1755. Chelsea, Man City, PSG among clubs chasing £25m defender labelled the ‘next Raphael Varane’

By Oliver Thomas | 09 Nov 2026 13:19

European giants Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and Manchester City are reportedly among a big list of clubs chasing Lens defender Pierre Ismaelo Ganiou.

Reigning Champions League winners PSG already have a wealth of defensive options at their disposal, but finding a long-term successor to captain Marquinhos, 32, may soon become a priority, prompting the club to keep a close eye on France's brightest emerging talents.

Chelsea and Man City, meanwhile, have both had their fair share of defensive issues this season, conceding 29 goals combined after 10 Premier League games, and may also consider delving into the market for backline reinforcements.

According to TEAMtalk, Chelsea owners BlueCo and City Football Group, the parent company of Man City, have been keeping tabs on 21-year-old Ganiou, while PSG are ‘fully aware’ of his potential.

Tottenham Hotspur, Newcastle United, Brentford and Fulham are said to be among the other English clubs to have watched the highly-rated centre-back this calendar year.

Ligue 1 duo Marseille and Monaco are also monitoring Ganiou progress, with Italian clubs Atalanta BC and Como, and Bundesliga pair Borussia Dortmund and RB Leipzig among the other European teams keeping a close eye on his development.

Ganiou has enhanced his reputation with Lens following a breakthrough period in French football, making his Ligue 1 debut in October 2025.

Widely regarded as Lens’ greatest-ever academy product, Ganiou is a physical, pacey and elegant centre-back who has been compared to former France and Real Madrid defender Raphael Varane.

The young defender's path to the first team was somewhat unconventional, involving temporary stints away from Lens at Annecy and Padova to bypass strict loan registration rules.

However, following his successful return, Ganiou made a massive impression during his debut season with Lens last season, with his rapid breakthrough convincing the club's hierarchy to reward him with a four-year contract extension over the summer.

Ganiou has made a total of 37 senior appearances for Lens in all competitions, with 29 of those coming in a memorable 2025-26 campaign that saw Les Sang et Or finish second in Ligue 1 and win the Coupe de France for the first time in the club's history.

The 6ft 1in defender worked under current Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage last season and has since established himself as a first-team regular, despite the early departure of Dino Toppmoller and arrival of Yannick Cahuzac as the club’s new head coach in September.

Valued at €30m (£25m) by transfermarkt and capped five times by France Under-21s, Ganiou is currently sidelined with a knee injury, but he hopes to be back in the first-team fold soon and continue his impressive trajectory as a core component of the Lens defence while interested suitors continue to watch on.

The Red Devils were rocked in September when Gabriel and his representatives made a bombshell request to have his academy contract torn up. Gabriel's dream is to win the Ballon d'Or, which was awarded this year to England's Harry Kane

#1753. Man City transfer news: Etihad player ‘finished’ under Enzo Maresca with January plans revealed

Manchester City defender Rayan Ait-Nouri is reportedly ‘finished’ at the Etihad Stadium having fallen down the pecking order under manager Enzo Maresca.

Ait-Nouri was signed by Maresca’s predecessor Pep Guardiola in the summer of 2025, joining from Wolverhampton Wanderers in a £31m deal and penning a five-year contract.

The 25-year-old left-back chipped in with five assists in 28 appearances for City across all competitions last season, missing the majority of December and January following his involvement with Algeria at the Africa Cup of Nations.

Ait-Nouri celebrated winning both the FA Cup and EFL Cup in his debut campaign with the Sky Blues, though he did not feature in either final played at Wembley.

This term, Ait-Nouri has struggled to force his way into Maresca’s first-team plans and is currently viewed as a third-choice left-back behind Josko Gvardiol and Nico O'Reilly.

Ait-Nouri is yet to make a single Premier League appearance for Man City in 2026-27, while he has made just two substitute appearances in the Champions League – his only two starts have come in the EFL Cup.

Although Ait-Nouri is said to remain keen to fight for his place at Man City, Football Insider claims that the defender has failed to make an impression under Maresca.

The report adds that Ait-Nouri is unlikely to play ahead of either Gvardiol or O’Reilly any time soon, and could therefore push for a move away from City during the January transfer window in search of regular first-team football.

Maresca recently admitted that Ait-Nouri is struggling for game time, telling reporters: "He's a clear full-back. In that position, we have [Gvardiol], who is doing fantastic, we have [O'Reilly], who when he is fit is doing fantastic; and he's the same position, so it's just competition between them."

A surprise transfer to City’s rivals Manchester United was mooted for Ait-Nouri in the closing stages of the summer window, and the possibility of the Red Devils making a January swoop is said to have been explored.

While agreeing personal terms would seemingly not be an issue for Ait-Nouri, who could be receptive to a switch across Manchester, it is understood that the relationship between City and United is the ‘main issue’ that could scupper this potential move.

Serie A giants Juventus have also been consistently linked with a move for Ait-Nouri and a switch to Italy is thought to be more realistic at this stage, though the Old Lady may prefer to negotiate an initial loan deal.

#1752. Messi was a deity among Argentina’s unholy rabble

Little sorcerer calls time on playing for his country six weeks after World Cup final defeat which was marred by brutality of his team-mates

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless New Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

And yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

“Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

You struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose

To study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

By Oliver Thomas | 09 Nov 2026 14:23

Scottish giants Celtic and a number of Championship sides have reportedly been given fresh hope in their pursuit of Chelsea starlet Kendry Paez.

Paez agreed to join Chelsea from Ecuadorian outfit Independiente del Valle in 2023 before his £17m transfer to the Premier League club was made official in the summer of 2025 after his 18th birthday.

The attacking midfielder experienced a disappointing loan spell at Chelsea’s sister club Strasbourg in France, before his January loan to River Plate was cut short in August due to a lack of regular game time.

Paez is now back at Chelsea but does not feature in Xabi Alonso’s first-team plans, with the youngster currently training and representing the club’s Under-21 side.

Celtic also sit top of the Scottish Premiership table as they bid to defend their title, but they are set to face stern competition from Championship teams for Paez, including current leaders Birmingham City and mid-table outfit Blackburn Rovers.

It is claimed that Blackburn were offered the chance to take Paez on loan in the summer and may get that opportunity again in January, while Birmingham are said to be prepared to consider a loan deal as they fight for Premier League promotion.

#1749. Why it's all gone wrong for Charlton: JAMES SHARPE reveals the summer failures, a player's mysterious disappearance and murmurs of yet another sale as Nathan Jones' side teeter on the brink

Published: 21:00 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 06:26 EST, 7 November 2026

Fear is creeping back in at the Valley. Charlton’s defeat by Bolton on Tuesday night, their fourth on the bounce, was greeted with the cacophony of boos it deserved.

Eleven games without a win and teetering above the Championship relegation zone. A fanbase that has been down this long and treacherous road before, and sure as hell doesn’t want to tread it again.

Certainly not when they thought those dark days were, at last, behind them. Only 10 weeks ago, Charlton sat top of the table after victory over Preston completed a hat-trick of early season wins, including a famous triumph in front of a record Championship attendance of 62,264 at West Ham.

It was a false dawn. For the first time under Nathan Jones, the ship has stalled and, for now, is going backwards.

Charlton looked destined for relegation to League Two for the first time in their history when Jones took over in February 2024. They went 14 games unbeaten and survived. After spending eight of the previous nine seasons in the third tier, he took them up via the play-offs at the next time of asking and, last season, kept them in the Championship.

For a club that had endured so much instability, a period of normality and steady progression was on the cards. Jones is Charlton’s ninth managerial appointment since June 2016. Only now, the wonder is how much longer this can go on before nine becomes 10.

Fear is creeping back in at the Valley with Charlton 11 games without a win and teetering on the brink of the Championship relegation zone

For the first time under Nathan Jones, the ship has stalled and, for now, is going backwards

‘If I hadn’t done what I’ve done at this football club, it would have been an easier decision for them (the owners),’ Jones told South London Sport this week. ‘I have to win football games. Win games or you don’t survive.’

His next chance is against ninth-placed Sheffield United this Saturday afternoon. Jones insists he maintains a strong relationship with the Charlton board. The new chief executive Ben Mansford – formerly of Leeds, Blackpool and Barnsley and who ended the club’s spell of 19 months without one – twice tried to hire Jones at his previous clubs. Jones is understood still to have the backing of his players.

Perhaps it’s not best to let him know that both Alan Pardew and Chris Powell lost their jobs after defeats by the Blades.

‘We've spent a lot of time in League One recently and I think there is a kind of head-in-hands worry at the moment: please let's not go back there again,’ Heather McKinlay, chair of the Charlton Athletic Supporters' Trust tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘At the moment, it feels more like duty than fun. I think we have become a little bit worn down because we've been through the mill so much with the changes of ownership and the shenanigans over the near 20 years since we were in the Premier League.’

They have been through the mill, much of the difficulties driven by those in charge. Former owner Roland Duchatelet, who still owns the Valley and the training ground, once accused fans of wanting the club to fail. Charlton’s fans responded to his comments and mismanagement by carrying a red coffin to the Valley followed by a crowd of mourners in a mock funeral protest against his ownership.

They lobbed hundreds of plastic pigs on the pitch for one game, beach balls to halt another, and sent a black cab to Belgium as a ’Taxi for Roland’.

Within weeks of Duchatelet selling Charlton to businessmen Tahnoon Nimer and Matt Southall for £1, the two new men were embroiled in a bitter public row. Nimer accused Southall of using club money to fund his own lifestyle, which he denied, including renting a £150,000-a-year flat in London and giving a fleet of Range Rovers to his associates. Charlton fans occupied the boardroom in protest. Thomas Sandgaard, the next owner, was arrested by the FBI this year and charged with fraud. He denies any wrongdoing.

The highly impressive win away to West Ham in August now appears to have been a false dawn

Jones is Charlton's ninth manager in the last 10 years - but how long can he keep this up?

‘Charlton fans are a proactive lot,’ adds McKinlay. ‘If they feel they can make a difference, they’ll do something. I don’t feel we can do anything right now other than cheer them on. I think the ownership want the club to succeed. The manager wants the club to succeed. The players want the club to succeed. There's not really a baddie in this.’

As one club insider put it this week, it’s nice, in a strange way, that football is the main issue for once and not what’s going on off the field.

There is still a sense of that, mind. The current ownership group known as Global Football Partners is made up of seven shareholders, each with more than five per cent, but it remains unclear who is the driving force. Sources suggest some are more willing than others to put their money in with murmurings that the club is once again up for sale. Charlton insist they are merely looking for more investment to help drive the club forward.

Poor recruitment has not helped matters either. All the talk in the summer was about ‘evolving’ from a team that could get out of League One, then stay in the Championship, to one that could compete.

The club, however, spent a net total of just £1.5million this summer. They failed to find the right winger they needed, as a deal for Crystal Palace winger Jesurun Rak-Sakyi collapsed late on. Instead they signed teenager Junior Nkeng, who hasn’t played a single minute. A lack of creative midfielder is glaring too.

As for those who did arrive, Millenic Alli infuriated supporters in the defeat by Bolton when he headed the ball blindly into no man’s land during stoppage time with the team desperately searching for an equaliser. Nathaniel Chalobah arrived as a free agent from Sheffield Wednesday with a reputation for being injury prone. He showed his class at the start of the season, got injured, returned and is now injured again.

That’s not to mention the bizarre mystery surrounding midfielder Timothy Ouma. The Kenya international, on loan from Slavia Prague, went off to play for his country during the recent break and has not been seen since. Ouma, who has not featured in a single matchday squad since the break, has previous for this, having also failed to return after international duty while on loan at Lech Poznan.

When Jones was asked about it a few weeks ago, he responded by saying: ‘We will address those rumours when they become relevant. Anything we need to put out, we will put out.’

Kenyan midfielder Timothy Ouma went off to play for his country during the recent break and has not been seen since

Nathaniel Chalobah (right) arrived as a free agent from Sheffield Wednesday with a reputation for being injury prone. He got injured, returned and is now injured again

Charlton remain tight-lipped on whether Ouma is still absent, though one insider admitted they still hadn’t seen him since the players returned from international duty. The Kenyan FA did not respond to requests for clarification.

It makes the decision to part ways with club captain Greg Docherty in the summer look even more misguided, with this a team lacking in leadership. Jones has been left to throw all the pieces up in the air and see where they land with constant changes to the team and the line-up. Selection and formation roulette, as some are calling it.

The Welshman is not everyone’s cup of tea, frequently mocked for his David Brent style, but there’s still a belief, not least from himself, that he can turn things around. ‘He’s a maverick, but he’s our maverick,’ laughs McKinlay.

Time is running out, though, because if Charlton cannot find their way again, the alternative is already too unnerving to think about.

#1748. The five Premier League managers under the most pressure - where does Michael Carrick rank?

By Joshua Cole | 09 Nov 2026 15:42

The November international break has arrived at a particularly uncomfortable time for several Premier League managers, with the opening months of the 2026-27 campaign exposing serious problems at clubs with very different expectations and ambitions.

While some teams have made encouraging progress, others have struggled to deliver consistent results, leaving their managers facing growing questions about their futures as club executives consider whether a change in the dugout could improve their fortunes.

Manchester United's Michael Carrick remains among the most vulnerable after another difficult start to the season, while Crystal Palace's Pierre Sage is reportedly on the brink of losing his position following Sunday's defeat to Liverpool.

Regis Le Bris, Matthias Jaissle and Oliver Glasner also entered the weekend under scrutiny, although their respective results have altered the immediate picture, with Sunderland and Nottingham Forest recording important victories against Chelsea and Manchester City.

With the Premier League now pausing for international football, Sports Mole looks at five managers who have had plenty to think about over the coming weeks.

Carrick's position at Manchester United remains one of the biggest talking points in the Premier League, with the former midfielder struggling to convince that he is the right person to lead the club out of its current difficulties.

United have endured a miserable opening to the campaign, with their 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on Sunday leaving them 18th in the table with just eight points from 10 matches.

Although rescuing a point after falling behind was evidence of some fighting spirit, the result extended their disappointing league run, with Carrick still waiting for his first Premier League victory since August.

The situation has been particularly concerning given United's status and the resources available to the manager, while their 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth and subsequent 2-0 loss against Chelsea have intensified scrutiny of his tactical approach and ability to get the best out of his squad.

Carrick retains considerable support among sections of the fanbase, which could work in his favour, but the club's hierarchy will be increasingly concerned about United's position in the relegation zone and the prospect of allowing the season to deteriorate further.

The Red Devils' dramatic comeback against Roma in the Champions League offered some encouragement, although the Premier League remains the priority, and the international break could provide United's decision-makers with an opportunity to assess whether he deserves more time.

Sage appears to be facing the most immediate threat of the five managers, with Crystal Palace reportedly preparing to part company with the Frenchman following their disappointing start to the season.

Appointed in the summer as Oliver Glasner's successor, Sage has struggled to reproduce the organisation and consistency that made Palace an established force under the Austrian.

Sunday's 3-1 defeat to Liverpool at Selhurst Park left the Eagles bottom of the Premier League table with seven points from their opening 10 matches, having recorded just two victories during that period.

Their defensive problems have been particularly damaging, with Palace conceding 24 goals, the highest total in the division, while their inability to turn performances into positive results has placed considerable pressure on their new manager.

The Frenchman's position has also been weakened by a lack of support from sections of the Palace fanbase, with the 5-0 defeat against Brighton earlier in the campaign providing another difficult moment during his short tenure.

According to reports, the club are now preparing to dismiss Sage, with the international break offering a convenient opportunity to make a managerial change without immediately disrupting the playing schedule.

Having inherited a difficult situation following the departure of Glasner and the loss of important players, Sage can point to mitigating circumstances, but the results have been insufficient to convince the hierarchy that he can turn things around.

Le Bris has earned considerable credit for his work at Sunderland, having guided the Black Cats to promotion before overseeing an impressive seventh-place finish in their first Premier League season back in the top flight.

However, expectations have changed following that achievement, and the Frenchman has discovered that maintaining Sunderland's progress is proving considerably more difficult.

The Black Cats entered the weekend in the relegation zone, with their performances and results raising questions about whether the squad had been strengthened sufficiently to cope with the demands of another campaign.

A 2-0 Europa League defeat to Dinamo Zagreb had also increased the pressure, particularly after Le Bris admitted that his decision to rotate the team had not worked as intended.

Nevertheless, Sunderland produced an important response on Sunday, beating Chelsea 1-0 to move up to 19th with eight points.

The victory should ease some of the immediate scrutiny surrounding Le Bris, although it does little to disguise the broader problems facing the club, particularly with a demanding run of fixtures awaiting them after the international break.

The manager's previous achievements should earn him patience, but Sunderland need to demonstrate that they can compete consistently rather than relying on occasional victories to keep their survival hopes alive.

Jaissle's position at Newcastle United is not necessarily as precarious as those of Carrick and Sage, but there are growing concerns about the direction of a club that expected to challenge for European qualification.

The German inherited a difficult situation following Eddie Howe's departure, particularly after Newcastle sanctioned the sales of several influential players, including Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes across successive transfer windows.

However, the significant investment made in replacements has not produced the expected improvement, with Newcastle struggling to establish a consistent playing identity under their new manager.

Their 1-1 draw against Fulham on Saturday left them 12th with 12 points from 10 matches, continuing a disappointing run that has included damaging defeats and unconvincing performances.

Jaissle has also faced criticism for Newcastle's approach in possession, with his explanation following the defeat to Everton that his players had resorted to too many long balls raising further questions about the team's tactical execution.

There are mitigating circumstances, particularly the scale of the squad changes and the limited time available to build a cohesive team, but Newcastle's underlying performances have offered little encouragement.

The international break gives Jaissle an opportunity to work on those problems, although a significant improvement will be required if he is to convince supporters and the club's hierarchy that he is capable of taking Newcastle forward.

Glasner's situation is an interesting one because, despite facing considerable pressure before the weekend, the Austrian has given himself some breathing space with an impressive victory over Manchester City.

Forest had endured a difficult opening to the campaign, with their lack of goals and inability to turn promising performances into victories leaving them 19th after nine matches.

Their attacking struggles were particularly concerning, although the underlying statistics suggested that Glasner's side had been unfortunate, with their expected points tally significantly better than their actual position.

The club's ownership structure also makes the situation uncomfortable for the manager, with Evangelos Marinakis having demonstrated little hesitation in making managerial changes when results have failed to meet expectations.

However, Forest delivered one of the weekend's biggest surprises by beating Manchester City 3-1 at the City Ground, with the result lifting them to 16th in the table on nine points.

The victory represents a significant boost for Glasner, particularly after a period in which questions were being raised about his team's attacking efficiency and ability to collect points.

Nevertheless, one impressive result will not completely resolve Forest's problems, and the Austrian will need to build on the performance when domestic football resumes.

With the club's ambitions and expectations remaining high, Glasner will know that continued improvement is essential if he is to avoid becoming the next managerial casualty in an increasingly unforgiving Premier League.

#1744. Dowman ban upheld, football’s rules need to change

Let’s start again with Max Dowman whose three match ban was upheld after Arsenal’s appeal against the red card failed. The club had made the bid on the basis of wrongful dismissal and excessive punishment, but the claim was dismissed by an independent regulatory commission who will publish their ‘written reasons’ in due course. Thanks for that.

You will already know I think this is too severe. I thought the sending off was harsh, especially with the video evidence that backed the appeal, and for a player to miss three games for what was such a minor reaction to a heavy challenge is really unfair. And I would say that if this were an Arsenal player or not. It’s another example of how we hear about the concept of player protection all the time, but the reality is there have been countless incidents which could have been used to demonstrate there’s a seriousness about that but it never, ever happens.

How absurd is it that Max Dowman will serve the same ban as Ryan Shawcross got for snapping Aaron Ramsey’s leg in two? Remember when Dan Smith launched himself at Abou Diaby’s ankle, putting him out of the game for 9 months and causing an injury so severe it plagued the rest of the Frenchman’s career? He didn’t even get a red card that day, so the next time you see Dermot Gallagher pontificating on Sky about how a referee got an obviously wrong decision right, apply that context (he was the ref at the Stadium of Light that day).

Football has a problem with actual violent conduct, but chooses to deal with it by trying to make us think performative infractions like Dowman’s are worthy of the same punishment as the acts of real violence. The dangerous tackles, the two-footed leaps (which seem to creeping back into the game a bit, probably because they’re not being punished), pushing an opposition player when they’re in the air, these things are not on the same scale. If what Dowman did is worthy of a three game ban, the next time someone goes studs first over the ball into the shins of their opponent, they should get ten games at least.

But we know that’s not going to happen. Almost as long as this blog has been going (coming up on 25 years now!), I’ve made the case for there to be a sliding scale of punishment for acts that meet the definition of violent conduct. Some things are just more violent than others, but as long as this blanket punishment of three games regardless of the seriousness of the incident is in place, the more those in charge do the game and the players a disservice.

Still, it is what it is now, and Arsenal will have to live without Dowman for the games against Liverpool, Hull City, and the away trip to Newcastle on the far side of the upcoming November Interlull. He could well have been involved at some point this weekend against Liverpool, but now we’re sweating on the fitness of Noni Madueke, with Eberechi Eze the only other option for the left hand side. There are some whispers that Christos Tzolis could be back in contention for Sunday, which would be a very welcome boost, but the forward line looks a bit light for a game of this significance.

Tuesday’s game against Fleetwood will live in the memory because of the giant killing aspect, but for two young Academy players, it’s a night that will hopefully be formative. For Dowman, whether you think what he did was worthy of a red card or not, there’s a lesson to learn about how you react. To be quite honest, I think there’s something to like about the way he was prepared to stick up for himself against a grown man who wanted to ‘leave a bit on him’, as they say. The talented players are the ones who get kicked most though, and it’s something he’s going to have to contend with as his career develops. Just ask Bukayo Saka. The two have plenty of time on their hands right now, and I’m sure it will be part of his footballing education.

The other player is Marli Salmon who probably should have done better on their goal, but for me is less culpable overall than some of the senior players who didn’t perform at the right level. Arsene Wenger once said:

You pay for the education of young players with points. If I play a 20-year old centre back, I know he’ll cost me points during the season and I have to stand up for that. A less talented 28 year old would cost me less points. However, by 23/24 you have a player.

Marli Salmon is 17. He didn’t cost us any points. There’s a long way still go in his development, but I’m sure with the coaching staff they’ll go over what happened against Fleetwood and he will learn from it. It is more difficult for young defenders than young attackers too. A mistake at the top end of the pitch, like Dowman scuffing a shot wide from a position he probably ought to score from, doesn’t feel quite as costly as a forward running off a young defender to score the opening goal of the game. But again, it’s all part of the process, every young player makes mistakes, it’s how you then use them to improve that counts, and I’m sure he’ll do that.

Right, let’s leave it there for now. #1743. Liverpool transfer news: Alisson makes feelings clear on Anfield future amid Flamengo links

By Carter White | 09 Nov 2026 15:43

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker has insisted that he wishes to remain at the club past the end of the current season.

The 34-year-old started his 10th Premier League contest of the campaign on Sunday afternoon, when Andoni Iraola's side secured a 3-1 success at the Selhurst Park base of Crystal Palace.

After a promising start to the fixture for the hosts, it was Liverpool's star attackers who took control of the contest, with Germany international Florian Wirtz netting his first top-flight goal of the term.

The Anfield club were unable to record their fifth clean sheet of the Premier League season due to an Eddie Nketiah spot kick in added time, however, Alisson produced a good display following recent links to Brazilian side Flamengo.

Clearly planning for a future without the veteran shot-stopper, Liverpool are supposedly eyeing a swoop for a keeper valued at just over £30m ahead of the two transfer windows in 2027.

After a positive performance in the victory at Crystal Palace, Alisson provided a definitive response when asked whether he wants to remain at Liverpool past the end of this season.

"Yes, in my mind. I am focused on playing every game but in my mind I am happy to stay. You know, that depends on a lot of aspects and different situations," said the 34-year-old.

‘But my will is to stay. I am happy here, my family is happy here. I am still hungry for titles and for delivering good performances. I still want to play at the top level for as long as I can. So that is my thinking on that."

Alisson's current deal at Anfield runs out at the conclusion of the current season, meaning that he will be free to discuss pre-contract terms with foreign clubs in the New Year.

However, the keeper later stated that his agent had commenced talks with Liverpool's hierarchy over a new contract, and it appears that the player is not interested in a potential departure.

After a number of error-strewn performances at the beginning of this campaign in the Premier League, many supporters were suggesting that Alisson's days as Liverpool's first choice were numbered.

That being said, the 34-year-old was mightily impressive in the recent success at Crystal Palace, making six saves and keeping his side in the contest during a difficult first period for the visitors.

Giorgi Mamardashvili is the clear second option at Anfield currently, however, it is plausible that the Georgia international fails to grow into a position to become the man in between the sticks for the long-term.

#1742. Arteta didn’t see the reaction to the reaction but reacts to the reaction to the reaction

Morning all, let’s do a bit of a Saturday round-up ahead of tomorrow’s game against Liverpool which we’ll cover in more detail then.

First, Mikel Arteta responded to the appeal against Max Dowman’s red card, and said:

We’re very disappointed, to be fair, especially with the reckless tackles that he receives – his reaction is minimal in relation to the action. We’re disappointed it hasn’t been overturned having watched it back.

We’ve put every argument on the table to make a case for it – not only the action that is so evident, but when you look back in slow motion, the previous action and Max’s action is clear. Obviously, we have a very different opinion. I think you also have to look at the context of the player, the age and what happened previously.

You already know what I think. Ultimately, there’s only one person who was in any danger of being hurt on that pitch on Tuesday evening, and it was Dowman himself. Arteta said:

It could have been really bad, and we’re lucky today that he hasn’t had a broken foot – that’s clear.

But as we’ve discussed this week, football’s attitudes to things like minor retaliation versus a ‘crunching’ tackle are a bit topsy-turvey, and Dowman is a victim of that. The fact they didn’t even reduce the ban, which there is definitely precedent for, suggests to me they have chosen to overlook what the replays show, and that’s quite disappointing.

Still, it was interesting to hear Arteta reference Dowman’s age when referring to this, then a bit later on suggesting that if he’s going to play with the big boys, he’s not going to get any special treatment because of how young he is. There’s been discussion and debate about the manager giving the 16 year old a bit of an earful on the sideline as he went off, but in this instance he stood behind his ‘tough love’ approach. Referencing the fact Dowman had been sent off for England U19s a few weeks ago for something similar, and the conversation they’d had in the dressing room before they went out, he said:

I haven’t seen the reaction to my reaction, whether it’s positive or negative. But you need to understand the context, the relationship that I have with him and what we discussed just before we went out.

You want to see the reaction of his teammates? When they have to play with 10, you want to see that? This is the environment and this is the reality. Otherwise we are in Disneyland, we are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League at this level and we look after him so much that you cannot imagine. But at the same time we are going to demand of him, like to anybody else, because he needs to earn the right to play. Otherwise the rest of the boys, what are they going to tell me? You need to be fair.

As I said yesterday, hopefully it’s a learning moment for Max, one he can carry forward for when he returns and beyond. Professional football is absolutely ruthless, there will be managers/players who will try and expose that youthful temperament again, and we know how they’ll do it. He’ll get kicked again, they’ll try and bully him again, but next time he’s got to remember that referees are more inclined to punish the guy who retaliates than the one who perpetrates the first offence. It’s upside down, of course, but that’s the environment in which we exist and one he’s got to get to grips with. I suspect that whatever your own view of Arteta’s reaction, that message will have been made loud and clear to Max Dowman this week.

Elsewhere, because this is very, very funny, Aston Villa say they’re going to take legal action against Jamie Carragher for some comments he made on a podcast. Via their official social media channels, they released a statement which said:

Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the club and its fans. Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football. Nassef Sawiris, chairman.

Apparently Carragher’s remarks were about Unai Emery potentially joining Man Utd, and pointing out that there is a kind of pecking order in terms of club stature. Which, regardless of the fact United are a mess right now, is unquestionably true in terms of the size of the fanbase, the history etc. Villa are a successful club with good history of their own, but United are – in this general context – a bigger club. Like Barcelona are bigger than Valencia, like Bayern Munich are bigger than Borussia Dortmund, like some side from the Isle of Man third division are bigger than Sp*rs.

How thin skinned and pathetic do the people running Villa have to be to take exception to something Carragher said, to then ruminate on it, decide that legal action is the best course of action, and then make it public? Genuinely it’s hilarious and embarrassing. Also, I’d be quite happy for Emery to take over at United. He’s done a fantastic job at Villa, but as Arsenal fans we know he’s exactly the man you need to take over a club that’s something of a sleeping giant and a mess on and off the pitch. Emery in at Old Trafford all the way, in my opinion. They’d be facing that side from the Isle of Man third division in no time.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. Happy Halloween, I hope your little visitors aren’t too scary later on, and that your dogs don’t freak out with the fireworks too much.

#1741. Derided Thierno Barry is no longer a source of frustration as star fires Everton to victory over Coventry on another big night for David Moyes amid Jack Grealish drama

Published: 17:29 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 06:27 EST, 7 November 2026

Maybe Everton should request to play under the lights every week. It certainly seems to push David Moyes' team to new heights.

Following hot on the heels of consecutive night victories over Newcastle United, Friday's 3-1 win against Coventry City was a reminder of why, under Moyes, there is renewed sense of optimism at Everton.

Up to fifth, above Liverpool, and in a Carabao Cup quarter-final at Fleetwood, it could prove to be a special season.

This always felt like a big task for Frank Lampard, back at Everton for the first time since his sacking in 2023.

Popular as the ex-manager may be, there's no room for sentiment, certainly not from Moyes on a night he took charge of his 592nd game, drawing level with Harry Catterick for managing the most games in the club's history.

He'll set it outright after the international break against Brentford and Keith Andrews, who was 21 when Moyes first took up the reins at Everton.

Thierno Barry (right) now has 10 goals this season after being widely derided in his first season on Merseyside

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall had been left out of the England squad in the morning, but refused to let it spoil his night

His side started impressively, fashioning three shots in the opening 10 minutes, before losing all momentum and allowing Coventry into proceedings.

It took going 1-0 down, to a soft Yann Gboho goal, for the hosts to come alive. Thierno Barry, so often the source of frustration last season, was magnificent and all but won the game with a five-minute brace in the second half.

The striker didn't score his first goal until December last season. This campaign, he's reached 10 before the second international break. Moyes joked post-match that Erling Haaland should watch his back in the Golden Boot race is starting to feel less absurd. Barry now sits joint second in the charts.

Both goals against Coventry came via back post-duels. The first he confidently headed past Carl Rushworth, before bundling in a second five minutes later.

The disgruntled home fans booed the team off at half-time, yet were jubilantly cheering and signing after Barry's brace. The Frenchman danced on the pitch at full-time and was serenaded by the South Stand.

'I don't see loads of young centre-forwards scoring loads of goals in the Premier League,' said Moyes.

'He's come in and has settled in a bit more. His language and communication is better and obviously he's worked to get himself into the positions to score.'

Barry wasn't the only Everton goalscorer, of course. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was not one of the three Everton players named in Thomas Tuchel's England squad on Friday - only Arsenal had more representatives.

EVERTON (4-2-3-1): Pickford 5; Rohl 5 (O'Brien 73min, 6), Tarkowski 5, Branthwaite 6 (Keane 89), Mykolenko 6; Armstrong 6 (Hackney 73, 6), Garner 6; Dibling 5 (Johnson 73, 5), DEWSBURY-HALL 8, George 5 (Alcaraz 90); Barry 8.

COVENTRY CITY (4-2-3-1): Rushworth 4; van Ewijk 5, Mfuni 6, Pinnock 6, Dasilva 6; Yirenkyi 6, Torp 6 (Grimes 86); Sakamoto 5 (Tchaouna 86), Rudoni 5 (Hamer 86), Gboho 6 (Thomas-Asante 73, 5); Awoniyi 5 (Cherif 87).

But the midfielder sent a pointed message to the Three Lions' boss with a superb showing that was capped with a late powerful goal to end the contest.

'It was a disappointing morning, I'm not going to lie,' Dewsbury-Hall told Sky Sports after the game. 'It's a massive dream to play for my country. I know I was close.

'Yeah, sad, but really proud of myself and how I have reacted. All I can keep doing is putting in good performances and hopefully one day I get the nod, because I'm never going to give up. I've got the mentality. I'll keep pushing and pushing and see what happens.'

'He's desperate to play for England,' added Moyes. 'You never know if England get a couple of injuries, or anything changes.'

What ended as a comfortable win could have been a different outcome had Jame Tarkowski been punished for a hair pull on Caleb Yirenkyi, or if Vitalii Mykolenko's tussle with Taiwo Awoniyi in the box had been deemed a foul.

Both were checked and cleared by VAR, as was a handball claim in the build-up to Barry's second goal.

'Tarky pulls on Caleb's hair, they [VAR] are saying it's not enough of a pull,' said an aggrieved Lampard afterwards. 'That's a hard area to be in. What is hair pull and what's not?

'I think Taiwo, on the edge of the box was a penalty. I feel there's a penalty by the time Myko's knee is in the back of Taiwo's knee on the line of the box.

'Then the Barry one is handball. He flicks it in [with the hand] with the final touch. Nothing went for us tonight.'

#1740. Forward line must step up to help deliver first Anfield win in 14 years

After a midweek journey to the north-west for the EFL Cup, we’re back in that neck of the woods today to face Liverpool in the Premier League.

The team news from the press conference was relatively promising, with Declan Rice, Riccardo Calafiori and Christos Tzolis all in training ahead of the game, and Mikel Arteta sounded relatively positive on Noni Madueke who missed out on the trip to Fleetwood Town. With Bukayo Saka out, and Max Dowman obviously suspended, he’ll start on the right and hopefully this run in the team will see him deliver a little more in terms of end product.

He got the backing of the manager beforehand, who said of him reaching his potential:

He has all the potential to do it, he has all the attributes to do it. He certainly has the will to do it because when you see him train every single day, he’s one of the players who enjoys the practice the most and wants to expose himself to all kinds of situations and actions. Now he needs to put the performance on the pitch.

Eberechi Eze should start on the other side, looking for his first Premier League goal contribution of the season, and I think the only other decision to be made is the construction of the midfield. Will it be Myles Lewis-Skelly or Bruno Guimaraes with Rice and Martin Odegaard? My own preference for a tricky away game is probably for Myles, because if you need to change something the Brazilian has attributes you can count on for that. However, he started him away in Munich, brought Lewis-Skelly on in his place when we were 2-1 down and that turned out all right. So, let’s see.

My guess is we’ll see: Raya, Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori, Rice, Guimaraes, Odegaard, Eze, Madueke, Havertz

After two goals in the first three games of the season, Kai Havertz has gone five without a goal in the Premier League, so today would be a good day for him to get back on track and to find some form again. I’d like to see him stay more central, to be something of a focal point rather than drift around the way he likes to. Perhaps when you face good centre-halves as he will today that’s part of how you disrupt them, but right now there’s real focus on our strikers and what they’re delivering (or not delivering as the case might be), and I hope that he, and Viktor Gyokeres when he gets a run later in the game, can produce what we need.

As for today’s opposition they’re still a bit of a work in progress under Andoni Iraola, but they seem to be getting to grips with what he wants. It took him a bit of time at Bournemouth, and the same seems to be true at Anfield, but Liverpool’s only defeat of the season was to Man City, collapsing late on after going down to 10 men. They have a couple of injuries, but in Alexander Isak they have a dangerous centre-forward in good form, and a player who has caused our central defenders plenty of problems in the past. Gabriel and Konsa will have to be at their best today, the sharpness of his movement in the box is really tricky to deal with.

It’s been 14 years since we last won away at Liverpool in the league, something Arteta views as a record to change:

It’s an opportunity. I came here and in many places we were 20, 22 years, 18 years without winning, and we’ve been doing all these things, so on Sunday, that’s the opportunity that we have.

Regardless of how you might feel about going out of the League Cup, you can be sure Mikel Arteta’s pride will have been hurt by both the defeat and the gleeful reaction to it in certain quarters. He will demand a response from his team today, and if that brings about a win at a ground that hasn’t been favourable for us in recent years, then you wouldn’t be at all surprised. Nevertheless, I think today will be a real test for two sides, neither of whom are in tip-top form right now, and two excellent coaches whose connection and friendship goes back years to add an extra dimension to proceedings.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning.
