#1739. Arsenal maintain perfect start but lack firepower of rivals

Bukayo Saka maintained Arsenal’s perfect start to the season, but Mikel Arteta appeared to acknowledge that the Premier League champions are in danger of leaving themselves short in attack.

There is still time for Arteta to add another forward to his squad and whether he does so or not could be important, with the transfer window closing on Tuesday night.

Having sold Leandro Trossard and with Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus on the verge of moves away, Arsenal appear light of forward options.

Lyon winger Malick Fofana has been offered to the club, but he is an underwhelming target given Morgan Rogers and Vinícius Júnior were pursued earlier in the summer.

“We are trying to improve the squad,” Arteta, the Arsenal head coach, said. “Until Tuesday night, we’re going to try to do that. I’ve been disconnected from the world for 24 hours because I think my energy and focus has to be on the match. I will give it [my energy] now.”

Asked if he currently has enough depth in forward positions, Arteta added: “It depends if everybody is fit or not. We know that the depth has to be really big when you are fighting for four competitions. So we’re going to try to do that.”

This was an Aston Villa team there for the taking after being gutted by their Premier League rivals and still waiting for new signings to be ready to play and gel.

But Arsenal made hard work of their victory and one senses there will be more games like this if Arteta has to rely on what he has already got until at least January.

Chelsea are showing they can score goals for fun having spent £117m on Rogers. Manchester City are strengthening their firepower with the signing of Iliman Ndiaye and Bradley Barcola has joined Liverpool. Arsenal have the defence and the midfield, but not necessarily the depth of quality in forward positions of their rivals.

0.52 - Arsenal faced the fewest shots (11), the fewest shots on target (1) and allowed their opponents the lowest xG (0.52) across the first two matchdays of the Premier League season.🔒 Locked. pic.twitter.com/blSUAeqoLb

Christos Tzolis is the lone attacking signing to date and there was evidence at Villa Park that it will be a risk to rely too heavily on the Greek winger.

Tzolis had made an exciting start to his Arsenal career in the Community Shield and the first Premier League victory over Coventry City, but he had to be taken off at half-time on Monday night.

The former Club Brugge winger not only lost out to Matty Cash, but was also at the centre of Villa appeals for him to be sent off.

Tzolis had already been booked for a foul on Cash, when, in the 36th minute, he appeared to foul John McGinn as Villa broke from the edge of their own penalty area.

McGinn appealed that Tzolis should have been shown a second yellow card, but referee Jarred Gillett let the Arsenal man off the hook.

Arteta was wise to take Tzolis off at the break and his replacement, Eberechi Eze, had a hand in what proved to be Arsenal’s 59th-minute winner.

Eze slipped in Riccardo Calafiori and Saka got in front of Ian Maatsen to poke the Arsenal full-back’s low cross into the net. Saka’s goal had been the first shot on target in the game.

"It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL

Just before the goal, Arsenal thought they had been awarded a penalty. Ross Barkley lost possession with a sloppy pass, allowing Declan Rice to advance towards the Villa penalty area. He played the ball through for Saka and Maatsen barged into the back of the winger.

Gillett paused before pointing to the spot, but a VAR check showed that Maatsen’s foul had taken place outside the penalty area and Martin Odegaard fired the resulting free-kick wide.

The goal and the overturned penalty were pretty much it for Arsenal in terms of threatening the hosts, for whom goalkeeper Zion Suzuki made his debut. Suzuki did not have much to do with his hands, but impressed with his distribution.

It was Villa who went closest to scoring in the first half, through one of the club’s five surviving members of last season’s Europa League-winning team.

Emiliano Buendia scored Villa’s second goal in the final against Freiburg and the Argentine rattled the Arsenal crossbar with a 20-yard shot that had beaten visiting goalkeeper David Raya.

Before then, McGinn had sent a shot over Raya’s bar and into the building site where Villa are redeveloping the club’s old North Stand.

Buendia, McGinn, Cash, Pau Torres and Victor Lindelof are the only Villa players to have started the Europa League final who have not left this summer.

Defender Ezri Konsa is one of Villa’s Europa League winners to have departed and he made his Arsenal debut as a late substitute. The defender received a mixed reception, as he was first booed by some home fans but was then applauded.

Other than hitting the bar in the opening 45 minutes, Villa squandered a chance for a quick reply to Arsenal’s opener when McGinn hesitated instead of shooting after being played in by Nicolas Jackson.

Jackson lasted 71 minutes for Villa in what proved to be a promising debut. In the first half, he raced away down the right before sending the ball across the six-yard box. But there was no team-mate on hand to convert.

One of Villa’s other summer signings, Alejandro Garnacho, is yet to make an impact for his new club. The Argentine got an earful from manager Unai Emery for not being ready to go on. He eventually replaced Ross Barkley, but could not help conjure an equaliser.

This is the start Arteta wanted. But, in attacking positions, Arsenal will finish the transfer window weaker than they started it if the club are not active in the final hours of the transfer window. And that could prove costly.

We lost. We competed well. They won the league last year. We are trying to build a team but a lot of positive things [beyond] the result. How we competed. How it was progressively better. We didn’t create clear chances. Some players made fantastic debuts. Suzuki and Jackson did very good work. I think it’s the first step forward and positive for the next matches.

Accepting this result, I think we had chances to draw the match but we are in our rebuild. It is the way [ahead for us] making these changes and I say to the supporters and players that the message is there in the way we played.

To lose one match is painful but after the pain we must try to get positive things, This is the reason I am optimistic. There are 38 matches we played two. We haven’t one point but we can get better hopefully. And we will get players [Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis].

We can feel confidence because how we want to build the team again is true, to compete like today.

I think the squad we have now is how we planned with the  players we wanted.

[Are you confident you have replaced the quality that has gone?] Yes.

I’m really happy. It’s a big win. It’s a tough place to come and earn the three points but I think we deserved it.

It was a game where 11 was not enough and the finishers came in and did a magnificent job to win it. I know how tough it is to win here.

Every big team struggles against them for the past four years because they are so good. They are well coached, have great players. Great in transition. The moment you lose the ball and let them run inside they are really dangerous but I love a lot of the things I saw from my team.

Ebs [Eze] creates the action that sees us win the game, Bruno with Mikel [Merino] in midfield changed the dynamic of it, Ezri [Konsa] really composed and calm with every decision he made and then Zubi… I’m really happy with all of them.

Every game in the Premier League it’s like [you’re saying] we have to win this game. We know the level. We know how difficult it is in this league.

[Can you sign Julian Alvarez tomorrow?] I don’t know. That’s for the people upstairs.

It was a very tough match. Aston Villa’s defensive setup made things difficult for us, constantly catching us offside. We couldn’t attack as comfortably as we did last week. But as you know, sometimes one goal is enough for us. We have a very strong defence.

Today, we were great out of possession too and didn’t allow transition attacks.

I keep my targets for myself. Every week I want to be there and try decide the game as that’s what I’m in the team to do. That’s my mentality.

[Have you seen Chelsea?] I’ve seen them. [What do you think?] We’ll see on Sunday.

Jamie Carragher explains how Arsenal broke Aston Villa down for their winning goal 🔎 pic.twitter.com/CAI8zhznrJ

Arsenal host Chelsea on Sunday at 4.30pm while Villa go to Hull City at 5.30pm on Saturday. It’s too early for a must-win game for Villa who showed some positive signs tonight but they could certainly do with one.

Arsenal win with a performance of efficiency and patience that emphasises their superiority when asked to grind out a result.

John McGinnis arguing the toss with the referee about his belief that he was fouled in the box in the dying seconds. It was outside the box and if Maatsen’s ‘tackle’ wasn’t a foul, neither was Gabriel’s.

Not sure the way of refereeing that lets a lot of calls go and waits for VAR is going to enhance the game.

Maatsen tackles Bruno Guimaraes in the Villa box with an ugly lunge in which he appears to scissor him, kicking his heel with one leg before knocking the ball away with the other but the referee deems it fair and VAR lets it pass, too.

Arsenal’s game management is working well as usual until Raya goes too long and the ball bounces through to Suzuki. But when he starts a counter-attack Alysson ends it with a dive and back come Arsenal.

Maatsen slides in late on Saka down the right, bypasses the ball and crashes into his shin. Yellow card.

Aston Villa probe but Arsenal hold them 30 yards from goal and when they do slide pass down the side of a defender for Buendia to chase, Bruno is ideally positioned to cover and make the block which he celebrates as if he were Leonardo Bonucci.

Eight minutes of stoppage time are signalled by the fourth official.

Suzuki races 15 yards outside his box to head a long pass away from Havertz to McGinn. Back come Arsenal after McGinn is squeezed off the ball but Wan-Bisska wins it back with a fine tackle. He is among the best one-on-one pure defenders in the league.

Zubimendi rattles Buendia’s bones in a crunching but legal tackle.

That was Rice’s last contribution as he limps off. He is probably OK but wise to withdraw him if he has had a twinge.

Maatsen drives down the left and cuts into the box. White leans into him, Rice guides him with a rigid left arm and the rampaging left-back loses his feet. Maatsen acknowledges Rice’s fine defending when he gets back up.

Quite a few outside observers questioned why Arsenal signed Konsa. This apparent injury to Mosquera is the reason. With Saliba out for months and Timber still struggling to regain his fitness, Mosquera was the only right-sided centre-back in the squad (unless they repurposed White, who is needed at right back).

Garnacho faces up Saka after being played down the left by Buendia but his cross is blocked by the goalscorer. Raya catches the resulting corner.

McGinn wipes out Merino from behind and is deservedly booked. Moments earlier Alysson was also booked for leaving one on Gabriel after the centre-half had cleared the ball, choosing not to put on the brakes and bodychecking him instead.

Unai Emery has just gone ballistic at substitute Alejandro Garnacho.

Emery clearly wasn’t happy with Garnacho not being ready to come on and let the Chelsea loanee know about it.

And Mosquera cannot continue having overstretched so it’s a debut for the former Villa stalwart who is greeted warmly.

Suzuki saves in a one-on-one with Havertz running through from 40 yards, waiting and refusing to go down and make things easy for Havertz, sticking up a right arm to block the shot. But he may have been offside which may mitiagte it in terms of not costing Arsenal anything but he really should have beaten the keeper.

Nice pass from Merino to set the hare running.

Barkley plays a diagonal pass across the turf out to Alysson on the right and he hares round Calafiori to cross from the byline but could not get the ball past Gabriel at the near post.

Now Maatsen goes flying but this time in the Arsenal box under a challenge from White that was a duplicate of the one 30 seconds before. ‘Premier League corrupt as f---,’ sing the Villa fans, ignoring the similarities between the two incidents. The defenders’ arms made contact with the attacking players but without the force to send them sprawling.

Havertz hits the deck in the Villa penalty area when challenged by Kamara as they fought for Odegaard’s scooped dink from the right.

Bruno Guimaraes and Mikel Merino are stripped and ready to come on.

Once again, it’s Riccardo Calafiori who opens up the opposition’s defence with his off-the-ball running. He is the one player in this Arsenal team who makes genuinely unpredictable and unexpected movements.

McGinn’s combination with Jackson looks promising and the centre-forward invites him to bullock forward down the inside-right channel with a clever pass but the Villa captain is soon swamped by yellow shirts and the ball gets stuck beneath his feet.

Gary Neville makes the fair point that one of Arsenal’s most unheralded qualities is their patience. Their confidence in their rock-solid defence does not make them reckless but they are always confident of finding a way. They trust the method implicitly.

Aston Villa 0 Arsenal 1 (Saka) Mosquera has the ball 25 yards out, left of centre, he strokes it to Eze who angles a pass to Calafiori running between Cash and Lindelof. He makes it to the byline and cuts back a low cross that Saka and Maatsen both lunge at and the Arsenal winger gets there first to turn it in.

"It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL

Rice, Eze and Odegaard stand over it. Rive walks away and Odegaard approaches the ball with a semi-circular run-up. He whips it over the wall and about a foot wide of the left post. Suzuki was stranded but no matter.

It was outside the box. Not all that sure it was a foul either. But Arsenal will have a free-kick.

Maatsen and Saka collide as they chase a Rice pass that Saka would never reach. Seemed to be outside the box.

It has been fairly dull fare so far as two systems and structures that cede little space clash.

Lindelof rises high to meet Rice;s dipping cross from the right as Havertz, on his shoulder, was poised to pounce. He heads it straight up and Suzuki leaps to catch it.

Now Barkley picks out a diagonal to send Jackson down the left. The centre-forward reaches the 18-yard line, cuts inside and works it over to McGinn who lofts a cross over Villa’s back-post runners and out of play.

Eze did his best work from the left last season. Villa start with Barkley scoop-chipping a pass from the middle out to the left, 40 yards upfield. Maatsen runs on to it and drives past White to ram a shot into the side-netting.

Arsenal were too slow to move the ball forward in that first half, and too loose with it when they did get into promising positions. There’s a lack of urgency in their passing. I wonder if we’ll see Bruno Guimarães soon… one of the reasons they signed him was to add more quick forward passing to their play.

Signs of encouragement for Villa without creating much while Arsenal have been stymied so far by Villa’s neutering of Tzolis and the left wing. Arsenal’s right-sided trio – White, Odegaard and Saka – look the most likely to create something.

Only a minute of added time to be played. Arsenal still lacking a spark, largely because there’s a lack of precision in their forward, line-breaking passing.

Villa will be very happy with this half. Much more like their old selves in terms of structure and organisation.

Calafiori’s throw to Gabriel is picked off by Jackson down the right and he dribbles down the right. He is forced to slow down to wait for a midfield runner. When Hemmings catches up, so have three Arsenal defenders and though Jackson bends in a low, cross to the edge of the six-yard box it is about 18 inches away from Hemmings’ reach.

Calafiori goes down in the Villa box when Pau Torres uses his arm to lever him away as they tracked the flight of a cross. The referee sees nothing wring in it and neither does VAR.

Gillett takes an age to stop the play when Cash uses his body to shove Tzolis over after the winger had played a pass. Cash obviously thinks he has rattled the new signing and is keen to rough him up some more. The ref does award a free-kick but only after that daft delay.

Tzolis loses the ball on the edge of the Villa penalty area, tackled by McGinn. The captain slots a straight pass up to Buendia who tries to bend a pass into Jackson’s stride as he sprinted down the inside right channel but Gabriel read the trajectory and got there first.

Suzuki picks out McGinn with a long pass. He feeds it to Buendia who gives Hemmings a chance to chase it down the left. Arsenal shuffle over in defence so he doubles back and returns the ball to Buendia. The No 10 whips over a dipping cross looking for Barkley and Jackson but Calafiori and Raya make sure the goalkeeper wins it.

We’ve not seen much from Christos Tzolis on Arsenal’s left wing so far. He’s been excellent since joining the club this summer but he’s hardly seen the ball in this opening half an hour and he’s just been booked after losing a battle with Matty Cash.

Arsenal free-kick 30 yards out, left of centre, for a foul on Lewis-Skelly who was artfully shielding the ball. Odegaard chips to the right post but Havertz heads it back across the box rather than going for goal and Villa clear.

Cash gets the better of Tzolis again in the tackle and then Suzuki sprays a perfect 60-yard pass out to Hemmings that Gary Neville, likening it to something Ederson was capable of delivering for Man City, one of the best goalkeeper passes he has ever seen. Tzolis was booked for stopping Cash running off with the ball.

Maatsen, who could never dislodge Digne for long, has a chance now to make the position his won. He strides down the left, exploiting Rice’s positioning error but his right-foot isn’t half as good as his left and his bending effort is scuffed far too straight and easily cleared.

Saka drives down the right after a neat Odegaard, Saka, White triangle. Pau Torres races over to toe the ball behind for a corner. Saka takes and Rice flicks it on at the near post and Suzuki tips it over. No corner, though, as Gabriel had rag-dolled McGinn at the back post after the Villa captain had backed in to him and tried to stop him making a run into the middle.

“Champions of Europe, you’ll never sing that.” Villa fans poke the wound.

Arsenal are finding it difficult to play through the middle of the pitch but have found Saka in space on the right wing on a few occasions already. Villa are congesting the central areas, where Odegaard does his best work.

Calafiori picks off Kamara’s pass looking, for the third or fourth time, to play someone, usually Jackson, in behind the left-back. A minute later Calafiori challenges McGinn for a bouncing, loose ball and stoops to use his head. colliding with McGinn’s boot. Was the head low or the boot high? Arsenal think the latter but the ref sides, rightly, with McGinn.

Arsenal corner on the left. The threat inherent every time Rice is in a quadrant diminished on this occasion because Mosquera barged Cash just after Rice struck the ball. Free-kick to Villa.

Timber may be preferred by Arteta at right-back but Saka prefers White. The two have a well-grooved partnership in tersm of who underlaps and who overlaps. They never seem to get in each other’s way.

Bukayo Saka does seem to be getting a lot of time and space on the right flank.

It’s looking a risky tactic by Villa at the moment as the England international is being invited to cut in towards the penalty area.

Havertz is played down the inside-right channel in the penalty area by a cute Odegaard pass bur he blazes his shot across goal and wide of the left post. A replay shows he was offside but even so it was a lazy finish.

Kamara grabs Tzolis round the waist from behind and when the winger hits the deck, rounds him and passus to Buendia who crashes a right-foot diagonal shot on to the bar from 20 yards. The ref did not see it as a foul despite Arsenal’s protestations but had it gone in it would have given VAR a dilemma.

Worth keeping an eye on Aston Villa midfielder George Hemmings tonight.

He is only a teenager and has emerged from Villa’s academy, but Unai Emery is already a huge fan.

Hemmings produced a highly promising performance in the Super Cup against Paris Saint-Germain earlier this month.

Suzuki misjudges the flight of Rice’s typically menacing corner and flaps at it but his defenders and an offside flag leave him without egg on his face.

McGinn stops Calafiori down the left then gives the ball straight to Tzolis. The Greece winger opens his body and passes to Lewis-Skelly who shoots with his right foot from the left of the 18-yard line. Cash slides in to block the shot and it loops over the bar for a corner.

Hemmings uses his strength to hold off Ben White and shift the ball inside to McGinn who wraps his left instep around a shot and wafts it into building site behind Raya’s goal.

Ibrahim Mbaye and Taylor Harwood-Bellis are in the directors’ box watching the game. Villa don’t look like a hastily assembled team.

Suzuki knocks the ball long with his left foot, looking for Jackson but the ball spins away from him to Raya who boots it back upfield. McGinn pounces on it, turns past Rice and plays Cash in down the right. He crosses towards the near post and Mosquera hooks it clear.

Arsenal kick off with Odegaard spinning and trying to play Saka in down the right as they defend the empty North Stand end. The ball skids off the turf and Saka can’t trap it. The ball goes out for a Villa throw-in.

Who dies in the summer and played for both clubs.

Arsenal are in fact in yellow and navy. My mistake.

Villa in claret and blue with a twist, the shorts are blue for the first time since, I think 2001. Arsenal are in yellow and black. Leeds, like Arsenal, have traditionally worn yellow and blue as their away strip but have been shunted into yellow and black as well by Adidas this season.

There are a few guys standing in the North Stand with hard hats on, and it appears they are on ball retrieval duty.

They will be on red alert for any wayward shots that land in the empty stand.

Warm reception for Ezri Konsa from Villa’s fans as he walked back to the tunnel with Arsenal’s substitutes.

Konsa joined Arsenal last week for £51m, ending a spell of seven years at Villa Park.

Wonder if the likes of Morgan Rogers and Emiliano Martinez will get a similar reception when they return here with Chelsea.

Aston Villa  Suzuki; Cash, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen; Kamara, Barkley; McGinn, Buendía, Hemmings; Jackson. Substitutes  Bizot, Mings, Ruggeri, Garnacho, Abraham, Bogarde, Wan-Bissaka, Edward, Lynch.

Arsenal  Raya; White, Mosquera, Gabriel, Calafiori; Lewis-Skelly, Rice; Saka, Odegaard, Tzolis; Havertz. Substitutes  Arrizabalaga, Hincapié, Eze, Gyokeres, Konsa, Madueke, Merino, Zubimendi, Guimaraes.

Zion Suzuki is one of two debuts for Aston Villa tonight and there is a genuine buzz of excitement around the Japan international.

Suzuki was signed from Parma for £30m as the replacement for Emiliano Martinez and arrives with a stellar reputation.

He’s got big boots – and gloves – to fill, but Unai Emery is convinced he will become a future star at Villa Park.

The other debutant is record £65m signing Nicolas Jackson, who joined last week from Chelsea.

Good evening. Yes, the first match was not as planned but we must keep going forward. Today we are playing our first home match and I am looking forward. We need to try as soon as possible to get our best individuals fit for a good performance. And today is a good match for us. Ir is difficult but always with our supporters here we feel comfortable and confident. Hopefully we can transmit our positive energy to our supporters.

We lost the first game but it is not a [team full of rookies]. We have experienced players. They play with energy and know how we want to play. We have to adapt with Suzuki but we have confidence [in him]. Jackson, the striker, and other players, George Hemmings, he is young but played fantastically in pre-season. He knows how we want to play.

Today is a challenge but I’m really looking forward to how the players will respond collectively, individually. We know we are changing things but no excuses. We have to perform today, we have to try to adapt the new players, to build our team to get their best today.

I am positive and I am optimistic. The players are ready.

Aston Villa are in a transition period and rebuilding on and off the field.

Unai Emery’s 2.0 have been under construction all summer and there could be 10 new signings in by tomorrow morning.

Villa have of course lost six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final, with Morgan Rogers, Ollie Watkins, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans, Emiliano Martinez and Lucas Digne all departing this summer.

The North Stand at Villa Park, which faces the iconic Holte End, is also under renovation and closed down for tonight’s game.

It could be a bit quieter tonight but there is still a mood of optimism among Villa fans, despite such a summer of change.

We have had a real block of training sessions to work on things and prepare for this game in the right way.

We will have time to make changes throughout the game [on why he has picked an unchanged team]. They did really well [against Coventry] and for the game we expect [tonight] they have the right qualities to hurt them and that’s how we start.

They have that [upheaval in personnel] but they have been with Unai for a long time, they are a super well-coached team and we know how tough it is always to come here. We are very conscious of that but also very ambitious.

That’s the way we want to play [with aggression] constantly from the first minute, to suffocate the opponent and be better than them.

[Does it being your 250th Arsenal Premier League game add something special to it?] Just to win [makes it special].

She wore… she wore… she wore a yellow ribbon …

Two changes – Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson make debuts. Joao Gomes misses the match as the first of his three-game suspension and Marco Bizot drops to the bench.

Double debuts 🤩Your Villa XI to face Arsenal this evening 👋 pic.twitter.com/Zue0ZTSJt9

Arteta names unchanged starting XI but Bruno Guimaraes is fit for the bench. Ezri Konsa joins him there.

🟡 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🔵Unchanged for Monday night football 🔐🤝 Presented by @deel pic.twitter.com/ptvpKHDahn

In its rightful place 🏠🏆 pic.twitter.com/FMH4zve1aD

Advertisement | GambleAware | 18+ Betting on the football tonight? Take a look at these tips and offers chosen by Telegraph Media Group

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Aston Villa and Arsenal from Villa Park. The champions travel to the team that finished fourth last season in buoyant mood and form despite some misgivings within their fanbase about their recruitment this summer.

It amounts so far to making Pier Hincapié‘s loan into a proper transfer, revamping the left wing with Christos Tzolis replacing Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli, upgrading options in central midfield by buying Bruno Guimarães and selling Cristian Norgaard – and signing Ezri Konsa from today’s opponents to give them the greatest elite defensive depth that I can recall at club since Manchester City’s Treble winners had Kyle Walker, Ruben Dias, John Stones, Nathan Aké, João Cancelo, Aymeric Laporte, Manuel Akanji, Rico Lewis and Sergio Gómez on the books at the same time.

Villa, by contrast, have endured a turbulent summer of trading with the departures of Europa League winners Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne, the aforementioned Konsa, Ollie Watkins and Emi Martínez, raising, along with other departures, more than £315m. They have spent about £180m to remodel the team though Johan Manzambi, who is injured, and João Gomes, who is suspended after his red card in the 4-0 defeat by Brighton, are absent tonight.

We can expect to see Zion Suzuki, Matteo Ruggeri and hopefully Nicolas Jackson and Leon Goretzka who have been registered in time to play, plus the loan signings Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho. Still to come are the pending purchases of Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Ibrahim Mbaye in a process that emphasises how profoundly Villa are invested in and dependent upon their manager, Unai Emery.

After so much upheaval, it would be foolish to set much store on Villa’s 2-1 victory last season, sealed by Emi Buendía’s winner in the fifth minute of stoppage time. Arsenal barely broke sweat in blowing Man City away in the Community Shield and cakewalked to victory over Coventry in the league’s opening fixture. His past work suggests Emery will be able to forge another formidable side from his talented new squad but this match feels two months too soon for him against his old club.

#1737. Genoa 1-2 AC Milan: Cisse and Pulisic score in hard-fought victory

AC Milan secured a much-needed three points on Sunday afternoon as they beat an in-form Genoa side 2-1 at the Stadio Luigi Ferraris.

The groundwork for the victory was laid in the first half, when Alphadjo Cisse slotted in a cut-back from Adrien Rabiot to get his eighth of the campaign, before Christian Pulisic buried a square pass from Gonçalo Ramos after a stray pass inside the box.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Ellertsson made it a very nervy finish for the Rossoneri with a goal inside the final few minutes from a long-range strike, but Milan did ultimately manage to hang on for what was an important three points.

It means that a top four spot has been reclaimed for the time being while waiting to see how the game between Inter and Como plays out, and it eases some of the pressure heading into the international break.

Ruben Amorim chose to make five changes from Thursday’s defeat to Ferencvaros. Mike Maignan, Mario Gila, Luka Modric, Diego Moreira and Christian Pulisic all came into the side, though there were some question marks about whether it would be a four or three-man defence based on the names selected.

Genoa started on the front foot and they immediately created an opening inside the first minute. Koni De Winter allowed Osmajic to run off his shoulder and get a shot off from the left side of the box, but Maignan watched it roll narrowly wide of the far post.

One minute after Vitinha had back-heeled a near-post cross into Maignan’s hands, Milan created their first opening. Pulisic’s cross from the byline wasn’t well-aimed but the clearance fell straight to Ramos, who didn’t quite connect right with his effort and sent it a couple of yards wide of the far post.

Milan continued to knock on the door and Ramos almost found himself on the end of a golden opportunity when Gila was found on the overlap and provided a cut-back, though Marcandalli did brilliantly to cut out the danger.

Then, in the 13th minute, Milan did take the lead through Alphadjo Cisse. The goal was assisted by Adrien Rabiot who found the run of the Italian with a nice square ball, but Pulisic was the one who won possession back on the high press to create the opportunity, which was well finished by Cisse for his eighth goal of the campaign.

In the 19th minute, the Rossoneri doubled their lead. Another successful press forced Ostigard into a mistake as his square ball back towards the goalkeeper was cut off by Ramos. The Portuguese squared to Pulisic after evading a defender, and the American made no mistake as he fired inside the near post to make it 2-0.

Right on the half-hour mark, Genoa thought they had got themselves back into the game when Osmajic headed past Maignan having escaped his man to be found by Vitinha’s flick-on. However, the offside flag was raised and the decision was upheld, though it looked very close.

Despite being two goals up, Milan never gave the impression of being in control and Genoa had a couple of half-chances towards the end of the half, including an Ostigard header that Maignan managed to claim.

The start to the second half was certainly a fractious one, and the Milan players were surrounding the referee Davide Massa five minutes into it when Rabiot seized on a loose touch from Marcandalli to run in behind.

He was dragged back by the defender who appeared to be the last man, but a yellow card was deemed to be sufficient. Rabiot got a yellow too for his protests, and three members of the Milan coaching staff were shown a red.

Amorim opted to make a couple of changes on the hour mark, with Cisse making way for Omari Hutchinson and Diawara coming off for Filippo Terracciano.

As the game entered the final 20 minutes, Milan began to look comfortable with their lead but at times complacent too. Musah gave possession away in the left-back position and it gave Vitinha a dangerous position to get a shot off, though Maignan did well to parry it away.

The pressure continued to come from the Rossoblu, and El Shaarawy had a chance off the bench when a cross found him in the box. He brought it down well, but Terracciano got a knee to it to deflect it over. Pulisic made way for Ardon Jashari after.

Inside the final few minutes Pervis Estupinan became the last player to come, replacing Musah. The sub was made just before El Shaarawy lined up a free-kick from about 22 yards out, and it would yield Genoa’s route back into the game.

The initial shot was blocked as it went into a crowd but was not cleared, allowing Ellertsson all the time in the world to step up and strike one from distance that nestled inside the right post with Maignan rooted. Game on with two minutes of normal time left.

Welcome to our Live Comments section, where new comments will appear automatically

The Rabiot-Pulisic-Cisse-Moreira midfield/wing attack is solid – Pulisic and Rabiot are the key connectors – without them on the field, we have trouble advancing the ball.

Magic Mike does enough to keep the scoresheet clean until the end.

Jashari a day late and a dollar short on defense, another instance of him not shutting down a shot on goal, allowing Ellerton to waltz down the field for a nice strike. Boy did we overpay.

Estupinan with a stupid foul that almost cost us the win.

Cisse is a great finisher but everything else needs A LOT of work. His passing is poor. Really poor.

Hutchinson and Jashari still 50-50 with their performances. after derby Diawara had a shaky game.

Ramos needs to start being the n9 we need him to be. 500 minutes for single G/A is not good. imagine how many games would have ended faster if he was able to k!ll the game.

our defending needs so much work… 13 goals scored on, most in top 5: – DeWinter is not CCB, will play way better as RCB/LCB. – Pavlovic is missed, today was a game where he would have been needed. – CCB like Renato Veiga would help a lot. – Chemistry with back 3 and wing-backs, also. their communication needs work. – LWB, once again our weakest role. can’t blame Musah for today. he was makeshift. Barte needs serious work on off-the-ball and generic defensive actions. Estupido needs to leave. along with Veiga, someone like Zalewski should be brought in and Alexis given more time there.

Maignan, Rabiot, Modric, Puli, Gila, Pavlovic are the only solid players we have. They show up every game and always game changers. Cisse, Ramos, Moreira need more work to stand along those 6. squad depth is definitely an issue with us.

I said this pre game start. The winner will be who can convert the chances. Luckily we were the most efficient because we only were able to shoot 2 on target and that’s it. 6 total shots. Genoa had double digit shots but were only able to convert 1 of their 5 on target. I am starting to get worried on our inability to attack all 90 mins. And our defence is shaky still once the subs come in

We need to break the bank there is no other choice. We brought a stubborn coach who needs ball carrying and great technics, which we don’t have that much. Bench lacks a lot of depth, we had to defend a goal lead with terraciano/Estupido on the same left flank… My absolute nightmare that almost cost us the game it’s insane!!!

Its clear our backup midfielders are not good enough, Both Jashari and Musah needs to be handheld in midfield and I trust neither of them in front of the defence. Musah’s awareness and reaction speed is next to zero and Jashari is casually at about everything, Might as well bring Comotto in at this point, atleast there is a unknown factor. But we seriously need to admit the attempt at reintroduce players like Estupinian and Musah was a mistake, which we already established last year.

Ramos is becoming a serious question mark, obviously some player take longer to settled and get going but at the end of the day when you are signed for a league record fee as a striker you gonna be judged by how many balls you put in the box.

Amorim need to figure out what kind of style he wants and stick with it, changing formation and approach to almost every game on top of heavy systematic rotations screams inconsistency.

If we are being honest, Milan’s two goals were ‘freak’ goals. On the first goal, Pulisic won the ball back on his own, then Ramos made a nice decoy run to open up space for Cisse. The second goal was a gift from Genoa. Milan’s offense created nothing the entire game.

Well, that’s the honest truth. We need either a good, creative playmaker/midfielder or proper tactics/ideas on how to attack. The “send a low cross into the box” -approach in the UEL showed how unimaginative and weak our attacking plays are.

#1736. Arsenal transfer news: Gunners 'targeting' world's most creative teenage defender

By Carter White | 09 Nov 2026 16:18

Arsenal-linked Ryan Augusto has topped an extensive list of football's most creative young full-backs.

Mikel Arteta's side extended their lead at the top of the Premier League standings with a 1-0 success over newly-promoted Hull City on Saturday afternoon, when Martin Odegaard netted the winner in the second half.

The Emirates contest saw the return of winger Christos Tzolis following an injury setback, with Arsenal supposedly eyeing up a move for RB Leipzig and Norway wide attacker Antonio Nusa ahead of the 2027 transfer windows.

The 21-year-old was particularly impressive against Manchester City in the Champions League last week and has also made a sensational start to the Bundesliga term, scoring four goals and providing seven assists across nine appearances.

The Premier League champions were known to be in the market for a high-profile forward player during the most recent summer window, missing out on the signings of Vinicius Jr and Julian Alvarez.

Always on the lookout for the next big talent, Arsenal were linked to Bragantino defender Augusto last month, with the youngster enjoying a breakthrough campaign in Brazil this calendar year.

Now, the 19-year-old has received a noteworthy accolade, placing top of a study based on creative full-backs and wing-backs under the age of 20 by the CIES Football Observatory, as relayed by Brazilian outlet Trivela.

Over the course of his 12 Brasileiro matches so far in 2026, Augusto has managed to produce 0.32 expected assists per 90 minutes - a figure greater than any of his positional counterparts across 52 top-flight leagues.

This clearly points towards the excellent attacking ability of the right-back, who is likely to secure a switch to a European club in the near future, given his undoubted potential.

Augusto also possesses the qualities to invert into midfield and combine with teammates in the centre of the pitch - a characteristic which would be helpful for Arteta's Premier League holders.

Conceding just five goals in 10 Premier League matches so far this season, Arsenal are undoubtedly the best defensive side in the division, as was the case last campaign when they beat Manchester City to the title.

A major part of that solidity, right-back is a position of riches for the Gunners, who have recently welcomed Jurrien Timber back to first-team action following a significant injury layoff.

There is also good reason to mention the contributions of England international Ben White, with the nonchalant character building an excellent relationship with Bukayo Saka on Arsenal's right-hand side.

#1735. Liverpool 0-1 Arsenal: Resolute Gunners dig in for a big Anfield win

Fourteen years is a long time to wait for a win at any stadium, but Arsenal ensured all three points returned from Anfield to North London for the first time since 2012 yesterday.

The surprise in the team line-up was the return of Christos Tzolis who had missed a month, more or less, with a hamstring injury. If it initially felt a bit harsh on Eberechi Eze, Mikel Arteta’s post-game comments about him barely making the game because of an injury problem of his own made it make more sense.

Early on, we were really good. Plenty of the ball, playing it well in their half, and lots of control. Liverpool looked a bit off the pace, and in the opening minutes young midfielder Trey Nyoni was lucky to escape without some sanction for a nasty foul on Martin Odegaard. I think it was much more mistimed than malicious, but studs down the Achilles is never good, and we saw Crystal Palace striker Jean Philippe Mateta see red for something similar on Saturday evening.

The early pressure paid dividends when Liverpool were a little sloppy at the back. Odegaard pounced to recover the ball, it was fed to Noni Madueke via Bruno Guimaraes, and when Declan Rice overlapped, his precision ball to the back post found Kai Havertz for a tap-in to make it 1-0. That makes it 5 assists so far this season for the midfielder, all of them from open play as well, and his presence in this team reminds me so much of Patrick Vieira. Not that they’re the same kind of player, but that his importance and stature is just fundamental to us. The desire he showed with that overlap is, essentially, what cracked this game open in our favour.

There was another back post chance for Havertz, almost getting on the end of a deflected Guimaraes shot, but after that – as happens so often at Anfield – the momentum changed. This time there was no Granit Xhaka style confrontation to act as a catalyst, the game just shifted and in the final 20 minutes of the first half we rode our luck a bit.

Liverpool started to play around our box and deliver dangerous balls. One almost found Alexander Isak but a combination of David Raya and Ezri Konsa was enough to see it trickle wide. Florian Wirtz hit the bar with a free kick, and Liverpool wanted a penalty when Tzolis looked to pull back Cody Gakpo but I don’t think there was enough in that one. The next one, however, oooof.

Liverpool put in another dangerous cross, Isak was there to head towards goal from close range, and Jurrien Timber’s shirt pull absolutely prevented him from making contact with the ball. You know my rule of thumb with penalties: how would I feel it were given, or not given, up the other end, and if we didn’t get that I’d be fuming. It’s a penalty all day long, and even if the ref didn’t quite see the foul well enough, the VAR officials really ought to have suggested an on-field review. I found the focus on Isak’s reaction a bit odd. Surely the onus is on the officials to recognise what we’ve all seen without a player having to prompt them in that direction, but we got so, so lucky there.

As we did when Alexis Mac Allister ran into the box and, unmarked from 10 yards out, headed the ball over the bar when he absolutely should score. That was a very bad miss from a Liverpool perspective, and a huge chance to equalise just before the break. We needed half-time, and despite the fact Liverpool enjoyed plenty of the ball in the early part of the second period, they looked a lot less dangerous.

My explanation for this is that we leaned into one of our great strengths, which is our defensive organisation and discipline. I thought Konsa was outstanding, but so too was Riccardo Calafiori at left-back whose one on one defending has improved massively. He dealt with Gakpo, he then had to contend with Rio Ngumoha, and I just loved the concentration as he focused on the ball and more often than not prevented Liverpool from creating danger.

Myles Lewis-Skelly came on midfield, Odegaard’s pressing was relentless, and as I remarked on BlueSky afterwards, if this team could attack half as well as it can defend, we’d be the best team in the world by a mile. There were moments when we could have countered better and with more pace, but we still found some threat in the second 45. The best chance fell to Tzolis, set up by Madueke, and his first-time shot was heading for the bottom corner but for a brilliant save from Alisson.

Liverpool threw the kitchen sink at it from the bench, but it made little difference. Mac Allister then got a bit naughty, slapping Odegaard on the back of the head, then collapsing to the ground to make it look as if Madueke had leaned his head into him. Replays showed that didn’t happen, and it was pretty pathetic from the Argentina international. I guess, as well as being a risible piece of play-acting, there was an element of desperation to it, because Liverpool huffed and puffed but could not blow our house down because of how defensively outstanding we are as a team.

For the first time in Premier League history, Liverpool finished a home game without a shot on target, which tells you something. It probably tells you just how much that Timber shirt pull had an impact because a striker like Isak would at least have tested David Raya from there, but more broadly it tells you that this is a team who look laser-focused on their target this season which is to retain the title – something we’ve never done in the modern era.

Afterwards, I thought the manager’s turn of phrase was interesting when he referred to it as ‘a mission’, saying:

Just loving the mission and the mission was something that we didn’t accomplish in 14 years. You really need to enjoy that. If you don’t, there will be a moment that you will switch off and they will punish you. I think the way we competed and played and the chances that we generated as well, it was really impressive so I’m really happy.

He’s obviously referencing winning away at Liverpool for the first time in such a long time, but I think it applies to the season as well. And, as I referenced in yesterday’s blog, there was a response to the midweek defeat to Fleetwood Town. If that was a result that as fans we could find relatively easy to compartmentalise, I don’t think the same is true for this manager because we know he wants to win every game, and it how much it stings when we don’t – especially against lower league opposition. He expected his side to deliver, saying:

It was a feeling, how the hell can that happen? How can you get out of the cup when you shoot 27 times? We had the chances that we had against a team that had put one shot on target and then you look so silly. Then you have to go to Anfield and say, how can I lift those players up? I had a feeling and I said, now is the moment. We’re going to have to dig deep, have an element of luck at times and for sure a lot of quality in the key moments and we’ve done it.

Which I think is a pretty fair assessment. We did a lot of stuff very well, we had moments of luck – which you so often need in a game like this to take all three points – but I don’t think anyone should be under any illusions that this was anything other than the champions demonstrating our title credentials again. In every season, regardless of how good you are, you need the rub of the green from time to time, like a Ruud van Nistelrooy penalty miss at Old Trafford, or Mateus Fernandes missing a huge chance for West Ham. It doesn’t change the inherent quality you possess or what you’re capable of doing, and in the cold light of day it should make you more driven to ensure you widen the margins – and by that I mean delivering a bit more in the opposition’s final third.

However, no complaints this morning. We had a job to do, and a difficult one at that, and we did exactly that to put us back on top of the table. It’s a nice place to be, but it’s still so early in the season I think we should dismiss any chat about what it means at this point. We can be impressed, but still cognisant of the fact there’s still a long, long way to go.

Right, I’ll leave it there for now, but we will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on today. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

The pod should be out around around noon or so. Until then, have a good one.

#1733. Fridges and pigs and scoring goals

We live in strange times. Sorry to start your day with this shocking revelation, I realise this is a bit of a bolt from the blue, but it’s fact. All across Europe supermarket fridges are being hacked. What a time to be alive. They used to hack, I dunno, mainframes and banks and shit, but now they’re hacking fridges.

Maybe they just got bored taking billions of made-up money from CryptoSloth and BitWomble and needed a challenge. I feel like fridges ought to be the kind of thing you just can’t hack – beyond unplugging it – but what do I know? Anyway, it’s an example of how the inter-connectivity that brings us all together every day is being weaponised and now the sliced meats in your local store are gone off because Neo pwned some large cold cupboards. As if we don’t have enough to deal with.

Such as all the people who hate the way Arsenal play. Let me be very clear, my days of caring what other people think about this football club, or pretty much anything else that’s important to me, are gone. It’s a waste of time. It’s a bit like quote that’s often attributed to George Bernard Shaw, which says ‘Never wrestle with pigs. You both get dirty and the pig likes it.’

I don’t think he actually said that, but I think we can all connect with the meaning. It applies so much to social media, and to many of the ways we’re exposed to punditry and ‘expert’ analysis in football these days. Like one of those shows where you have a couple of ex-pro pigs bleating on about this and that, and then a collection of other little pigs who support all the clubs argue with them and amongst themselves, and it’s just a pigstravaganza of pointless, inane bollocks but it does #numbers on socials so is seen as valuable #content.

I understand why opposition fans go on and on about how much they hate how Arsenal play. It’s because we win a lot of games. That’s the thing that really irks them. That’s just so basic though, you can’t appear to be clever and an aficionado of the game if you just say ‘I don’t like it when they win’, so it’s dressed up as dismissal of style or something else.

And look, here’s where the strange world we live in comes back into focus. You can, and really should, be able to hold more than one thought in your brain – about football or anything else – that holds true. I absolutely love how good we are defensively. LOVE IT. The commitment with which we are determined not to give the opposition anything is truly something to relish. Players laser-focused on their one on ones; putting bodies on the line to block shots and crosses; 11 players moving like a murmuration of birds because they’re so well drilled and organised; off the awareness and discipline; brilliantly timed tackles and headers and clearances; lads sticking up for each other when the opposition get a bit snide, as we saw on Sunday with Jurrien Timber and Noni Madueke refusing to allow their captain to be treated that way; it’s all part of a brilliantly defiant defensive attitude that runs right through this team.

Creating that is not easy. As Arsenal fans we have endured defences that were porous and feeble and, at times, very, very stupid. I do not long for a return to those times. Over the years Mikel Arteta has assembled a collection of players who cannot wait to go out there and do the dirty work of defending, and it runs from front to back because that’s what he demands. If it was that easy, everyone would do it, so to castigate a team’s brilliance in one department because you just lost to them without a shot on target just comes across as sour grapes.

Here’s the other thought though. I’d really like us to be a bit better from an attacking perspective, and when I look at this team and what it’s capable of, there’s no question the forward line remains the area where you can see the room for improvement. We defend as well as we do because, more often than you or I might like, we have to – because we live through games of fine margins. A 1-0 to the Arsenal is part of our history, hard-wired into our supporter DNA (particularly if you’re of a particular vintage), but I can’t lie and wish there weren’t a few more 3-0s to the Arsenal.

I’m absolutely certain Mikel Arteta would like that too, and I think it’s a bit too easy to say that this is a team that plays precisely the football he wants it to play. He is, as we all understand, an arch pragmatist, so what we get is a team that leans into its strengths, as laid out above. He is characterised as a defensive coach, which I get, but a few seasons ago we found an attacking cocktail that drove a title challenge, and saw us score more goals that year than the Invincibles did when they won the league in 2004 (91 to 73).

I think he wants both. He wants that parsimony at the back and the firepower up front. Unfortunately, forward line recruitment is the most difficult part of transfer business, and while he as manager has a part to play in that, as a club our track record is quite poor in that regard. This summer’s window was a complete bust from an attacking perspective, not a good look when you’re pursuing players like Morgan Rogers, Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez. When you then let three forwards go and add just one, there are questions to be asked of the people in charge. Arteta among them, of course, but he’s not the one whose job it is to get the deals done.

It’s why there are so many conversations around January, and what we might do. We see other clubs recruit forwards who produce on a consistent basis, while ours too often struggle to find that end product. Is it our system? Would these players find it hard to get those goals for us? Reasonable questions, but the bottom line in my opinion is that we have A+ options at the back and in midfield, while in that front three we’re a bit C-. That’s where the room for improvement is, that’s where the recruitment needs to be better (certainly better than no recruitment at all), and that’s how the games we currently win by a single goal margin, often by virtue of our defensive strength, become a bit more routine.

Simplistic? Yes. Easier said than done? Quite probably. But necessary? Absolutely. Until then though, expect more defensive masterclasses, more pig wrestling, and perhaps someone could hack our own Swedish fridge into scoring a few more goals. Worth a try!

Right, I’ll leave it there for now. I just have a small favour to ask. Arseblog has been nominated for Best Fan Media (Fran Merida) in the 2026 FSA Awards. We’re trying to retain our title, so if you could take a moment to give us a vote that would be much appreciated. You can do that here – https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/fsa-awards-2026

#1732. Nicolo Tresoldi: Italy call-up “a possibility” as Roberto Mancini issues update amid Germany competition

By Oliver Thomas | 09 Nov 2026 16:38

Italy head coach Roberto Mancini has provided a fresh update on the national team’s hopes of persuading Nicolo Tresoldi to represent the Azzurri over Germany.

The 22-year-old Club Brugge star was born in Cagliari to an Italian father and Argentine mother of Italian descent before he moved to Germany at the age of 13 for his mother's work.

Tresoldi joined Hannover 96 at youth level before spending three years in the senior team between 2022 and 2025, making 80 first-team appearances.

The striker has since elevated his game to new heights in Belgium with Club Brugge, while he has represented Germany at Under-19 and Under-21 level, scoring 19 goals 35 appearances across all tournaments.

Tresoldi’s standout performances have sparked a dual international tug-of-war between Italy and Germany, and he is still undecided on his long-term allegiance.

However, Mancini is optimistic that Italy can secure Tresoldi’s services following a conversation he and Claudio Ranieri - the technical director of the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) - had with the in-demand striker.

Speaking at a press conference on Monday ahead of Italy resuming their UEFA Nations League campaign this week, Mancini told reporters: “I have spoken to [Tresoldi], as has Ranieri. He needs to feel that he wants to play for Italy.

“Given that he was born in Italy and his father played for Italy [and won the European Under-21 Championship], I think there could be a possibility.

“Ultimately, it is the player who has to make the decision. He knows that we believe he could be important for us.”

Tresoldi has once again been called up to Germany’s Under-21 squad for the November international break ahead of friendly matches against Belgium and Croatia.

The next international break is scheduled for the end of March 2027, giving Tresoldi plenty of time to mull over whether he wished to represent Italy or Germany - now managed by Jurgen Klopp - at senior level.

Both Italy and Germany are understandably keen to win the race for Tresoldi, who has established himself as one of the most prolific strikers in Europe over the last 12 months or so.

Last season, Tresoldi inspired Club Brugge to their 20th Belgian Pro League title after scoring 13 goals in 30 matches to win the division’s Golden Boot award.

He has since carried his prolific form in the new campaign, netting 14 goals in 17 appearances across all competitions, including eight strikes in 11 league games.

Tresoldi is currently the joint second-top scorer in the Champions League with five goals in just four matches, including a memorable hat-trick in a thrilling 4-3 away victory over Inter Milan last month.

Known for his elite penalty-box movement and high-intensity pressing, Tresoldi is understood to have caught the attention of some of Europe’s biggest clubs, including Premier League champions Arsenal.

Manchester City, Manchester United, Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur have also been credited with an interest in Tresoldi, who is valued at €35m (£29.2m) by transfermarkt and is under contract at Club Brugge until June 2029.

#1731. 'People keep telling me it's great I'm managing against my son... it's not - it's horrible': Peterborough boss ROBBIE SAVAGE and Reading star CHARLIE on their 'awkward' FA Cup showdown, playing for Man United and dangers facing modern young players

Published: 02:00 EST, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 09:02 EST, 7 November 2026

The FA Cup cast its spell upon the Savages while they were out shopping for groceries.

Reading midfielder Charlie was strolling the aisles of the Marks & Spencer foodhall with his girlfriend when his phone began to buzz. He remembered it was first-round draw day.

He fished out the phone, saw the cascade of messages and realised, as they like to say in M&S, this was not just any FA Cup draw. He called his dad.

Peterborough United boss Robbie was in the Co-op. He had stopped on his way back to the rented lodgings he describes as a 'little annexe in someone's garden' and was rummaging through the ready meals in search of a spaghetti bolognese for one when he answered.

'The reception in Peterborough isn't great, it kept cutting out,' Robbie tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Charlie said: "You won't believe the draw." I thought he was going to say Forest Green. Or Macclesfield. I didn't think about Reading. He said: "You've got us." I just went: "Oh no."'

They were on a collision course from the moment Robbie left Forest Green for the Posh job last month. The teams were scheduled to meet in League One next month at Reading but the FA Cup draw caught them off guard.

Peterborough boss Robbie Savage (right) with his son, Reading midfielder Charlie. The pair will meet in the FA Cup first round at London Road on Saturday

'This will be the first time I hope my son doesn't have an impact, which is a horrible feeling,' Robbie tells Daily Mail Sport

And while they were both at great pains to stress that Saturday's tie at London Road, screened live on TNT Sports, is about Peterborough and Reading not their little family gathering, they can appreciate the fuss.

'Football is a beautiful game, it brings people together and creates rivalries,' says Charlie. 'This week it's created a rivalry in our family. I'm not sure who my mum, brother, grandparents and cousins will support but there's no better time for them to have a half-and-half scarf.'

For Robbie, the beauty of the occasion is yet to unfurl itself. 'It's going to be horrible,' he says. 'Every time I watch my sons play, I'm anxious. I'm nervous. I want them to do well. If they give the ball away and the other team attack, I've got butterflies thinking, "Please don't score".

'This will be the first time I hope my son doesn't have an impact, which is a horrible feeling. People keep telling me it's great. I've got to say it's not great, it's horrible. Usually we speak every day and I've not been able to speak to him all week because I don't want to put him in a position where anything gets out and anyone can point a finger at him.

'I don't want it to be billed as Savage v Savage because it's not. Charlie might not play but if he plays and makes a mistake and we score the winner, so be it. If he plays and scores the winner, well, wow.'

Robbie puffs out his cheeks and widens his eyes as he considers this scenario. 'We've got to win for Peterborough United,' he adds.

Ironically, it was a passion relit by coaching his sons which tempted the former Leicester, Birmingham and Blackburn midfielder out of the comfort of his media work and into coaching. Savage helped out with his youngest son Freddie's Under 13s team in the Timperley and District Junior Sunday League.

'Standing out at training on a Tuesday and Thursday night,' says Robbie. 'Sunday morning, putting the nets up. I've been that dad. In the first season we were hammered 13-0, but we built a team and won a lot of things.'

Charlie Savage in action for Reading. The midfielder played 45 games for the club last season but has yet to start a league match during this campaign

Savage offers some advice to his team in his new role as manager of Peterborough

Two years ago, Charlie and Freddie implored their father to follow his heart and make the switch from sporting director to manager at Macclesfield in the Northern Premier League.

'Even back then, he said one day he'd manage against me,' Charlie tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I was in League One and he was in Step Three and I'm thinking, "Well, give it a few years", but he always gets where he wants to get to.

'He's a competitor. He wants to win, wants to succeed. Even with my little brother's team it hurt him to lose in Sunday morning grassroots football. That's something inside him and it won't change.

'He will want to beat us. Unfortunately for him, I'm the same. I want to win. There might be an awkward car journey home.'

Charlie's memories of his father playing football are from Derby, the last stop of a 15-year professional career which started at Manchester United and took in seven different clubs, as well as 39 Wales caps. 'I remember seeing his long hair, scurrying around the pitch,' says the 23-year-old. 'Throwing his arms up and shouting at the refs.'

Like his dad, Charlie also came through United's youth ranks and made one first-team appearance, as a substitute at the age of 18 against Young Boys in the Champions League. It was an unforgettable night for Robbie, who was on co-commentary duty with a lump in his throat.

'He'll always have that on me,' says Robbie. 'All I ever wanted to do from 14 to 19 was play for one minute in Manchester United's first team. It didn't happen and he's done it. His name is on the wall at Carrington and mine isn't.

'I'm so glad his name is there instead of mine. You want the best for your sons. I'm proud of both my sons.'

Charlie has three Wales caps and counting. His father won 39...

...but despite both Charlie and Robbie coming through the Manchester United academy, only Charlie played for the first team (above), against Young Boys at Old Trafford in 2021

Freddie is studying for an economics degree at the University of Manchester. Charlie left United for Reading four years ago and now has 175 senior appearances and three Wales caps under his belt and a reputation in his own right.

'He's got a great left foot, passing range and incredible running ability,' says Robbie. 'He's intelligent. Nine As in his GCSEs. He doesn't drink, he lives his life 24 hours a day, seven days a week to be a footballer. He's a down-to-earth, humble kid.

'He was so brave to go and play senior football when he had three years left at Manchester United, and it's paid off. He played 45 games last season. He hasn't started a league game this season but hasn't sulked.

'I was a sulker, as Martin O'Neill and Nigel Clough (who coached Savage at Leicester and Derby respectively) will tell you. If that was me, my body language would be negative, but he's got a great attitude. And I've tried to tell him now he has to train harder than ever and conduct himself in the right way.'

If Robbie is a guiding light and inspiration for Charlie, vital information flows both ways for an aspiring manager with a young team.

'The mindset of a Millennial is completely different to when I played,' says the 52-year-old Posh boss. 'If they're not in the team or the manager has shouted at them, they go home to an apartment where they live alone away from their families, isolated from 2pm to 7am with all that time to think about it.

'We have to understand their vulnerabilities on and off the pitch. Charlie has been through that so without knowing it, he's made me a better manager. I try to think about what's best for my players, what I'd want a manager to do for Charlie in that situation.'

'He gives it out and he can take it and, unfortunately, it has become part of his life to be on the receiving end,' Charlie says of his dad Robbie

'Great left foot, passing range and incredible running ability,' says Robbie of his son Charlie

Being the Son of Sav cannot be easy. Not only the added scrutiny and expectation, and accusations doors have been opened for him by a famous and influential father, but also in a world where footballers are too often considered fair game for abuse whether inside the stadium or online.

'It's there in all forms of life,' admits Charlie. 'Maybe people subconsciously want me to fail a little bit more because of who he is. I get it. Football is a game and my dad is a divisive figure inside that game.

'He gives it out and he can take it and, unfortunately, it has become part of his life to be on the receiving end. Sometimes the abuse goes too far. People forget he's a human not just a football personality.

'But I wouldn't change who he is. I wouldn't change having him as my dad, I'm very proud of him.'

#1730. Saliba returns with scope for rotation against Slavia Prague

Arsenal are in Champions League action this evening, away to Slavia Prague. There was a big boost ahead of the game with the return of William Saliba to full training, and the Frenchman is with the squad for the game this evening. Whether he starts or not is another question, but he’s clearly in good enough shape to be in contention for some minutes, and that can only be a good thing.

It was obviously a topic of conversation at the manager’s pre-game press conference yesterday evening, and provided an update on how the recovery has gone:

He’s in a really good place. I think the process and the timings and in the manner the injury has been dealt with, and especially the feelings that Willy has been having along the way, they’ve been very, very positive. So, his evolution has been as expected, which is not always the case. He feels very comfortable. He played 45 minutes behind closed doors last week and he feels ready to go. So whether we use him or not now is a matter of what the team needs.

There have rightfully been plenty of plaudits for Ezri Konsa since his arrival, and the way he’s slotted into the team, and there was a question about how he solves the two into three ‘problem’ when choosing his central defenders going forward:

So far we haven’t had that luxury, I wouldn’t call it a problem! We can talk about problems that are very different to that one. The moment that they are fit and available, we’re going to have the opportunity to give players rest or to load the players and to manage the congestion of the players in a much better way than we’ve actually done.

That is most definitely the kind of problem any manager would like to have. There’s no need to rush Saliba back, we can be cautious with his reintegration, and then when we have the problem of deciding who plays in which game, it feels very much like the kind of bridge we can cross when we come to it. But it’s a very nice bridge.

Beyond that, I think there’s some real room for rotation this evening. Players like Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie will be looking for minutes at the back, and if we don’t see either Declan Rice or Martin Odegaard in the starting line-up this evening, I’d be absolutely fine with that. The manager can choose two World Cup winners in midfield, and still leave out one of Myles Lewis-Skelly or Bruno Guimaraes if he does that – it’s the kind of ‘luxury’ he needs to lean into.

Speaking about Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi, he said of their involvement so far this season:

They are playing a pivotal role. If we focus on the players that are starting, obviously that’s something else. Mikel has started some games already, some important games and he’s coming from a World Cup, a very successful World Cup. We know the value of the players that we have in the squad. They need to feel important. I do think that they feel very important and we have to make sure that they continue like that because if they have that spirit and that belief within themselves every time they play, they will make things happen for the team to win the game.

Up front, it’s a little trickier. Eberechi was a doubt for the game against Liverpool, while Christos Tzolis player almost the full 90 after his return from injury. I wonder is there any scope to start Max Dowman on the right, which means you can time-share the left between the two I just mentioned and/or Noni Madueke. I think you also have to look at this as another chance for Viktor Gyokeres who did get on the scoresheet against Fleetwood, but on a night when any kind of confidence boost that might have provided was offset by the fact we lost to lower league opposition. His minutes have been a bit scarce so far this season, but you’d be very hard pressed to argue that when he has played he’s done enough to give the manager much to think about. He could really use goals and a decent performance this evening.

I suppose that defeat to Fleetwood might give Arteta some pause for thought when it comes to how much he might rotate, but if you can’t give players minutes in games like this, then they’re not going to be in the kind of shape you need them be in if and when they’re required for more challenging fixtures. It’s not to take anything for granted against a side who are top of their domestic league, but in Europe this season they’ve been a bit poor, and if this isn’t the time to test our squad depth, I don’t know what is. Let’s see!

Before we go today, Andrew Allen has a feature in his weekly Patreon newsletter which covers match day recommendations. It started with restaurants/bars etc close to the ground, but has expanded over time into something much more global. With the help of @bootifulgame.bsky.social – they’ve built a really cool interactive tool which you can check out here – https://matchday.arseblog.com/ – and which now exists as a permanent feature on this site.

We often get questions about ‘Where can I watch with Arsenal fans when I’m in X city’ etc, and there are already lots of places listed around the world. If you want to add to the map, you can submit a recommendation to show where your local bar or venue is, and if you’re travelling somewhere, this is the perfect reference for when there’s an Arsenal game on and you want to hang out with fellow fans. It’s real community project, designed to bring supporters together, and which can improve over time with your help.

I’m sure it’s going to be really useful, and we’ll try and build it into the apps going forward too.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. As ever, we’ll bring you live blog coverage of the game later, as well all the post-game stuff on Arseblog News like the match report, player ratings, manager reaction, quotes round-up and more. Don’t forget the updated Arseblog apps also have a cool new matchday centre, full of stats, alerts, and much more.

#1729. Player Ratings: Genoa 1-2 AC Milan – De Winter, Pulisic and Rabiot take charge

AC Milan responded to the criticism with an important win at Genoa on Sunday afternoon. A few players made the difference and below are the ratings for the Rossoneri.

After the mid-week failure against Ferencvaros, Milan knew that three points were more or less a must against Genoa. Thankfully, aside from a dramatic ending, it was a comfortable game for the Rossoneri and a few of the players also got to send some strong signals.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

If you haven’t already, make sure to check out how we decide the player ratings. From the scale to what affects the rating, we have compiled everything there.

🥇 Pulisic (7.5 – MOTM): He did really well to keep his composure after receiving the ball from Ramos, making things comfortable with a two-goal lead. He was also the man who won back the ball before the first goal. In addition to the goals, it felt like he was always available and definitely helped Milan keep possession.

👎 Hutchinson (5.5): He was the worst for me, as he didn’t really add anything in attack and also failed to run down the clock at the end. It’s a shame because there was space to exploit when Genoa pushed forward.

👔 Amorim (6): Fielding Musah on the left actually worked out well, so kudos for that one. The rest of the eleven pretty much picked itself and tactically, while it was a good game, it wasn’t anything extraordinary. But his pre-match message seemed to work, as the players showed more desire.

Maignan (6.5): We saw a couple of good stops from him, including one on Vitinha in the second half, and his distribution was decent. He couldn’t really do anything about the goal either, as it was a really good effort from Ellertsson.

Gila (6): I liked his performance overall but there were a couple of moments that dragged down the rating for me, more specifically the fouls he committed. Put simply, he was a bit too rash and it was after one of the free-kicks he caused that Genoa scored their goal.

De Winter (7.5): The only poor moment came inside the first 60 seconds, when he was caught out a bit by a ball over the top, but he managed to track back and at least narrow the angle. After that, he was brilliant in his positioning, showing off with some great tackles and interceptions too. Really good.

Diawara (6): He was carded for a very rash challenge, but apart from that, he kept his calm at the back and had decent positioning throughout. It’s not like Genoa threatened Milan a lot, but enough for a pass here still.

Moreira (6.5): It was a lively start from him, I would say, with some good moments on that right flank. However, the end product wasn’t always amazing (some blocked shots), and he faded a bit attacking-wise as the game went on. Solid though and he did put in a defensive shift at the end.

Modric (7): We got to see some really nice flicks and quick play from him today. Defensively, he contributed as well, which was especially clear with a last-ditch toe-poke to avoid a 1v1 for Genoa. There was one poor pass into the middle which could have proved costly, but the rest was good.

Rabiot (7.5): He was back to his usual self today after what was a subpar display against Ferencvaros. Great movement between the lines and elegance on the ball were his main strengths, also getting the assist for the opener.

Musah (6): We have to praise him for doing well in a ‘new’ position, following the instructions from Amorim nearly perfectly. What stopped him from getting a higher rating here was the big giveaway at the end, which Genoa really should have done more with.

Pulisic (7.5 – MOTM): He did really well to keep his composure after receiving the ball from Ramos, making things comfortable with a two-goal lead. He was also the man who won back the ball before the first goal. In addition to the goals, it felt like he was always available and definitely helped Milan keep possession.

Cisse (7): It was a very tidy finish to give Milan the lead, showing once again that he knows how to turn up in the right place at the right time. However, for a higher rating, I would have liked to see more in his 1v1s, which weren’t always so successful.

Ramos (5.5): I’m torn here. It was unselfish to pass to Pulisic for the second goal rather than shooting himself, so that deserves praise. However, I actually think he was very sloppy in open play with heavy touches and positioning that sometimes left a lot to be desired. I suppose the big question is how much his defensive work rate is worth to the rating.

Terracciano (6): Surprisingly good! He had a crucial deflection on a shot from El Shaarawy and also headed the ball away quite a few times in the end, certainly contributing to the three points.

Hutchinson (5.5): He was the worst for me, as he didn’t really add anything in attack and also failed to run down the clock at the end. It’s a shame because there was space to exploit when Genoa pushed forward.

Jashari (6): We didn’t see much in terms of attacking contributions and build-up, since he came on with ten minutes to go, but he was responsible for a few clearances at the end.

Estupinan (5.5): I don’t think it was much of a foul, but in those moments, you shouldn’t even give the referee the opportunity to blow the whistle. He knows that.

Amorim (6): Fielding Musah on the left actually worked out well, so kudos for that one. The rest of the eleven pretty much picked itself and tactically, while it was a good game, it wasn’t anything extraordinary. But his pre-match message seemed to work, as the players showed more desire.
